World.title: Why public servants have less than a month to update pension records
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Public servants given until August 14 to update pension records [File]

Government has directed all public servants to update their records with the Public Service Superannuation Fund (PSSF) by August 14, 2026, in the latest step towards modernising pension administration.

In a circular signed by Principal Secretary for Public Service and Human Capital Development Dr Jane Imbunya, all PSSF members are expected to update their personal information and beneficiary details through the PSSF Member Self-Service Portal or the PSSF Mobile Application.

The circular was addressed to Ministries, State Departments, Constitutional Commissions, Independent Offices, County Public Service Boards and County Governments.

The exercise is expected to streamline pension administration and accelerate the processing of retirement benefits supported by a new Pension Administration System (PAS), a digital platform developed by PSSF to deliver faster, more transparent and more efficient pension services.

The registration exercise targets 529,635 members drawn from across the public service, including 332,950 teachers under the Teachers Service Commission (TSC), 120,084 officers in the disciplined services, 60,322 employees in Ministries, Departments, Constitutional Commissions and Agencies (MDCAs), and 16,279 county government employees.

PSSF Chief Executive Jonah Aiyabei said updating member records is critical to the success of the pension reforms and the delivery of efficient retirement services.

“By updating their records, public servants will enable quicker processing of retirement benefits, reduce administrative delays, improve data integrity, allow members to access pension services seamlessly through digital channels and ensure that the right benefits reach the right beneficiaries at the right time,” he said.

Under the new system, members can access their pension statements in real time, monitor contributions, view projected retirement benefits, update beneficiary nominations and personal details and initiate and track pension claims remotely.

The platform also features a Sponsor Portal that enables employer institutions to submit payroll information, contribution schedules and member data electronically, significantly improving efficiency and accountability in pension administration.

Dr Aiyabei said the Pension Administration System marks a significant milestone in the government’s efforts to digitise pension administration and restore dignity to retirees through faster, more accessible and transparent services.

“It will provide our members with real-time access to their pension information, enable seamless engagement with the Fund and support a fully digital, paperless pension administration process. Ultimately, our goal is to restore dignity in old age by ensuring every public servant receives timely and efficient pension services,” he said.

World.title: Inside Kenya's Ebola defences as seven Americans enter quarantine
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

A doctor provides care to a patient with Ebola virus disease at the Rwampara Ebola Treatment Centre (ETC) in Bunia, Ituri, July 13, 2026. [AFP]

Seven American humanitarian workers are spending 21 days under medical observation in Kenya not because they are ill, but because they could become ill.

A Reuters report published today confirms they are seven American Disaster Assistance Response Team (DART) staff from the Christian humanitarian organisation Samaritan's Purse . Franklin Graham, the organisation's President and CEO, confirmed this, saying:

“Samaritan's Purse has seven American Disaster Assistance Response Team staff members there. None of them have any symptoms, but they are being quarantined by the Kenyan government for 21 days."

The aid workers, all returning from the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), where they were involved in responding to the world's largest recorded outbreak of the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola, have no symptoms and have not tested positive for the virus.

Yet under new US public health rules, they cannot travel home immediately. Instead, they are completing a precautionary quarantine on Kenyan soil.

Their arrival has reignited debate over Kenya's role in regional outbreak preparedness and raised a question that extends far beyond the fate of the seven Americans:

If Ebola crossed Kenya's borders tomorrow, is the country ready?

The answer, infectious disease experts say, lies not in panic but in years of quiet preparation that most Kenyans have never seen.

That preparedness became evident during a recent visit by The Standard to Kenyatta National Hospital (KNH), where access to one of the hospital's high-security isolation areas was restricted.

Hospital officials informed the reporting team that patients with Mpox were being managed in the unit and, for safety reasons, journalists were not allowed to enter or film inside.

The brief encounter offered a glimpse into the strict infection prevention measures that underpin Kenya's readiness for dangerous infectious diseases.

According to an infectious disease physician at the Kenyatta National Hospital and head of the isolation ward, preparedness is far more than having an isolation room.

"One thing we should never do as Kenyans is panic," he says. "Panic only makes the situation worse. Instead, we should ask ourselves one question: Are we prepared?"

His answer is unequivocal. "As a government and as health institutions, we are in preparedness mode."

Dr Nyukuri explains that preparedness begins long before the first patient arrives at a hospital.

It means evaluating whether enough trained personnel are available, whether laboratories have the necessary testing reagents, whether protective equipment is adequate, and whether health workers understand every step required to safely manage a suspected Ebola patient.

"Here at Kenyatta National Hospital, we have conducted extensive training for healthcare workers," he says. "We have carried out readiness assessments, simulated patient scenarios and practised every stage of care from the moment a suspected patient arrives, through admission, isolation and treatment."

The simulations, he explains, are designed to ensure that no decision is being made for the first time during a real emergency. "When we eventually encounter a suspected case, it should not be something new to us." Dr Duncan Nyukuri, an Infectious Diseases specialist, during an interview with The Standard on July 16, 2026 at Kenyatta National Hospital. [Benard Orwongo, Standard]

Preparedness also extends beyond hospitals. Health surveillance teams remain stationed at airports and land border crossings, screening travellers arriving from affected regions while rapid response teams stand ready to investigate suspected infections.

"So far, Kenya has done a good job," Dr Nyukuri says. "We have not recorded a confirmed case despite the increasing numbers in the DRC. We pray that remains the case. But if we receive one patient, we are prepared."

How Ebola jumps from animals to people

Although Ebola is often associated with outbreaks, the virus begins its journey quietly in nature.

Dr Nyukuri explains that fruit bats are believed to be the natural reservoir of the virus. "They carry the virus without becoming sick themselves," he says.

Problems arise when increasing human activity brings people into closer contact with wildlife.

Mining, logging, hunting, charcoal burning, expanding settlements and encroachment into forests all increase the likelihood of viruses crossing from animals into humans.

"We call these zoonotic diseases," Dr Nyukuri explains. "Once the virus infects a human being, it can then spread from person to person through contact with infected body fluids, leading to outbreaks within families and communities."

You see, Ebola is a family; many people speak about Ebola as though it were a single virus.

In reality, scientists recognise five different species.

The best known is the Zaire strain, responsible for the devastating West African epidemic between 2014 and 2016.

"It is highly infectious and highly deadly," says Dr Nyukuri. "But because we have studied it extensively, we now have licensed vaccines and effective treatment options."

The Sudan strain, which has repeatedly caused outbreaks in Uganda, is the second most significant.

The current emergency, however, involves the Bundibugyo strain, first identified in Uganda's Bundibugyo District.

"This is the third recorded outbreak caused by Bundibugyo," Dr Nyukuri explains. "We have not studied it nearly as much as the Zaire strain."

There is currently no licensed vaccine specifically targeting Bundibugyo Ebola.

Instead, researchers are evaluating experimental vaccines while clinical trials in eastern DRC are testing promising treatments, including the monoclonal antibody MBP134 and the antiviral drug remdesivir.

"That is why this outbreak concerns many of us," he says. "We still have limited tools compared to what exists for the Zaire strain."

While Kenya has not recorded a confirmed case linked to the current outbreak, neighbouring countries remain on high alert.

Uganda on Thursday declared its last Ebola patient and has begun the mandatory 42-day countdown required before the country can officially be declared Ebola-free.

In contrast, eastern DRC continues battling sustained transmission, placing enormous pressure on treatment centres and frontline health workers.

It is against that backdrop that Kenya has found itself playing an increasingly important role in regional preparedness.

Their presence has nevertheless fuelled public debate over Kenya's preparedness infrastructure and the country's place in global health security.

Earlier this week, two American humanitarian workers who contracted Ebola while working in eastern DRC were medically evacuated to Germany for specialised treatment after receiving initial care in Bunia. Their evacuation underscores an important distinction: Kenya is currently serving as a precautionary observation site for exposed but healthy personnel, while confirmed Ebola patients requiring advanced clinical care have been transferred to Germany.

For Dr Nyukuri, the conversation should remain grounded in science rather than fear.

Preparedness, he says, is not measured only by isolation wards or specialised equipment, but by the ability of an entire health system to detect threats early, respond quickly and protect both patients and healthcare workers.

"My prayer is that Kenya never records a case," he says. "But preparedness means planning for the day you hope never comes."

As seven healthy humanitarian workers quietly complete their quarantine in Kenya, that preparation is no longer an abstract exercise.

It is being tested in real time. The development has also drawn attention to the contrasting roles played by East African countries during the current outbreak.

Uganda, widely regarded as one of Africa's most experienced countries in responding to Ebola, recently brought its own outbreak under control and has now entered the 42-day countdown required to be declared Ebola-free. Over the years, the country has built a reputation for rapidly detecting cases, tracing contacts and isolating patients, earning praise from the World Health Organization for repeatedly containing outbreaks before they spread widely.

Yet despite that experience, Uganda did not become a destination for foreign humanitarian workers requiring precautionary quarantine or post-exposure observation.

Instead, that role has fallen to Kenya, where seven American aid workers are now completing a mandatory 21-day quarantine after working in Ebola-affected areas of eastern Democratic Republic of Congo.

The contrast raises broader questions about how countries are selected to support international outbreak responses. While Uganda has demonstrated its capacity to treat Ebola patients within its own borders, Kenya's involvement appears to reflect a different function—serving as a precautionary observation site for exposed personnel rather than a treatment centre for confirmed cases.

Health experts caution against interpreting the distinction as a measure of either country's clinical capability. Instead, they say such decisions are often influenced by a combination of bilateral agreements, operational logistics, evacuation arrangements and the specific objectives of international public health partners.

World.title: Iranians warned that petrol prices may rise
World.content:
Amid high inflation and widespread damage to infrastructure, the Iranian government has warned that heavily subsidized petrol prices may have to be raised.

The issue is a sensitive one among Iranians. When the government raised fuel prices by 50% in 2019, nationwide protests quickly escalated into broader anti-government unrest and were met with a sweeping security crackdown and an internet blackout.

A change in petrol prices or fuel rationing is certain, government spokeswoman Fatemeh Mohajerani said Saturday, according to Iranian state television.

“We certainly need strategies for managing gasoline consumption because, as we know, the government is naturally subsidizing the price at which gasoline is sold to the public,” she said.

“It is obvious that a solution must be adopted to balance gasoline consumption … As for whether it will involve changes to the quota or to the price, the public will certainly be informed carefully, transparently, clearly, and honestly,” Mohajerani added.

Petrol is sold in Iran using three different tiers. Last December, the government introduced a higher rate for drivers consuming more than 160 litres (42 gallons) of petrol per month.

The head of Iran’s state fuel distribution company also warned of shortages in an interview on Sunday.

If high fuel consumption continues and production and import constraints persist due to damage to facilities, “it may become necessary to adopt measures aimed at maintaining the stability of fuel supply and the country’s energy security,” said Mohammad Sadegh Azimifar, CEO of the National Iranian Oil Refining and Distribution company.

Speaking to the news outlet Khabaronline, Azimifar acknowledged the sensitivity of the issue.

“The government will not catch people by surprise over petrol. If any decision is to be made, it will first be announced publicly, public opinion will be taken into account, and only then will implementation take place.”

World.title: What went wrong: How an OpenAI model went rogue
World.content:
When biologists experiment on dangerous viruses, they do so under strict regulations to prevent leaks or escapes.

But no such rules exist to prevent AI agents from similarly escaping – even though the consequences could be catastrophic.

That’s not a theoretical concern: An OpenAI test model escaped its test environment this week and broke into a real company’s servers when attempting to ace an internal cybersecurity evaluation.

And unless AI companies crack down on their testing safeguards, including training AI models on ethical task-solving, experts say more cybersecurity incidents will happen.

OpenAI president Greg Brockman told CNN at a press conference on Thursday that the company is still doing a “full investigation” to “understand everything that happened.”

“This is something to take very seriously, it is something that we’re looking at every single piece of our pipeline to think about the right ways to respond,” Brockman said.

The Sandbox

An AI sandbox is a confined environment companies use to test AI models; it’s meant to keep anything within it contained and separate from the rest of the world. Companies will often remove an AI model’s internal safety guardrails in the test environment so that they can evaluate its full capabilities while keeping it siloed off.

But in this case, OpenAI’s sandbox was not completely cut off from network or internet access, Jessica Ji, a senior research analyst at Georgetown’s Center for Security and Emerging Technology, told CNN. OpenAI said that the models had very limited network access duringt he test so they could install resources from internally hosted third-party software.

Using a previously unknown vulnerability in that software, the agents found a way to the open internet and then ultimately to Hugging Face, an AI opensource model and data set platform, through stolen credentials and other vulnerabilities.

Ji pointed out that OpenAI and the third-party software company were not aware of the vulnerability that allowed the model to escape, proving how important it is to fully scour a system for any potential exploits.

The Hugging Face logo on a smartphone on August 17, 2023. Gabby Jones/Bloomberg/Getty Images

It’s not the first time an AI model has broken out of its sandbox. Anthropic earlier this year said it instructed a model to do just that. But when it successfully escaped it then emailed an Anthropic researcher, even though it was not supposed to have that capability.

But the situation with Hugging Face is one of the first publicly disclosed instances of an AI model escaping its sandbox and hacking into another company’s systems – a task it was not specifically instructed to complete.

Ji said companies should be more aggressive with sandboxing their test models.

“That might require flying engineers out to a data center and having them plug into the network versus trying to trying to run things on the cloud or in a distributed virtual environments, like people are used to,” Ji said.

Companies should also have the option to manually turn off a model’s network access as a failsafe when testing risky scenarios, like evaluating whether an AI agent can hack a bank, Ji added.

Anything to reach the goal

A common technique in training AI models is reinforcement learning, or rewarding the model for completing tasks.

But the models will often do anything – including unethical steps like hacking – to do that. All the frontier models that the United Kingdom’s AI Security Institute recently tested attempted to cheat at least some of the time.

AI models only consider the consequences of their actions if they’re trained to do so, said Justin Cappos, a cybersecurity professor at New York University. For example, if you were told you had to come up with $10 million by the end of the day, breaking into a bank vault would complete that goal, even if you’d get arrested later.

“It’s very spooky. We have real evidence now that misaligned AI systems will essentially commit crimes, unless there are strong safeguards in place,” said Steven Adler, former head of product safety at OpenAI who now runs an AI safety group called Guidelight AI Standards. “We need to treat this like the warning shot it is.”

This week’s hacking incident has supercharged demands by AI researchers, cybersecurity experts and lawmakers for regulation of the rapidly advancing technology.“I figure a lot of people are on very urgent phone calls,” Ji said.

The problem, Cappos said, is that there’s a global race to dominate AI and make models that can improve themselves. Regulations could slow things down.

“So there’s a strong incentive for them to not have security controls unless their competitors also have those security and safety controls,” Cappos said. “This is this is the fundamental dilemma.”

World.title: ‘Up in smoke’: Attacks on ‘Russia’s Amazon’ bring Putin’s war closer to home
World.content:
A series of Ukrainian strikes on the warehouses of Russia’s largest online retailer has sent potentially hundreds of millions of dollars in inventory up in flames, sparking an online furor among the country’s embattled small-business owners.

Over the weekend, Ukrainian drones hit Wildberries distribution centers in Elektrostal in the Moscow region and Kotovsk in the Tambov region. A second wave of attacks early Wednesday hit logistics warehouses in the Krasnodar and Stavropol regions, while state media in the southwestern Voronezh region also reported that a drone strike forced the closure of a Wildberries warehouse there late Wednesday into Thursday.

On Friday, Ukrainian missile and drone producer FirePoint said Ukrainian FP-1 drones struck two additional Wildberries logistics hubs in Russia – the Shushary logistics complex in St. Petersburg and the Utkina Zavod facility in Leningrad region — and the company’s Simferopol logistics hub in Russian-occupied Crimea. Wildberries said Friday that the center in Simferopol had been evacuated and operations at Shushary and Utkina Zavod had been temporarily suspended.

The strikes on Wildberries, Russia’s equivalent to e-commerce giant Amazon, have brought Moscow’s war on Ukraine even closer to home by disrupting the lives and livelihoods of ordinary Russians. And they intensify a Ukrainian campaign of economic warfare that has seen wave after wave of long-range drone strikes on refineries that have caused long lines at the pump across Russia.

Local residents walk past the smoke of a fire at the Russian e-commerce firm Wildberries’ logistics complexes in the town of Elektrostal outside Moscow on July 18. Tatyana Makeyeva/AFP/Getty Images

The attacks have also been deadly. According to regional officials, seven people were killed in Kotovsk and one was killed in Elektrostal. At least one person was killed in the latest strikes in southern Russia, according to the governor of Krasnodar region.

Kyiv has acknowledged carrying out the attacks on Wildberries warehouses – and has said the facilities are legitimate military targets because they supply Russia’s frontline troops in Ukraine. In a statement Saturday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said – without naming Wildberries – that “major logistics facilities were hit” and that those warehouses were being used “to supply sanctioned components for drone production and navigation equipment.”

The Russian government denies that Wildberries supplies the Russian military. A search for “military supplies” on the Wildberries website Thursday yielded over 78,000 items, including body armor, first aid kits and rations. The site also offers drone equipment, including FPV goggles and kit that can be used on the battlefield.

The Kremlin did acknowledge the economic damage inflicted by the strikes. In response to questions on Wednesday about potential measures to protect businesses affected by the strike, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said of Wildberries, “the situation is indeed difficult given the losses suffered by both the company itself and small and medium-sized businesses.”

The economic impact of the strikes is not yet clear. The Russian edition of Forbes cited preliminary estimates suggesting Wildberries lost up to 9% of its warehouse space and that restoring that capacity might cost the company as much as 33 billion rubles ($421 million). Losses of sellers’ goods, the report said, could run at least to 150 billion rubles ($1.9 billion). The business daily Kommersant estimated the combined drone attacks affected about 10% of the company’s total logistics capacity.

CNN has reached out to Wildberries for comment on the financial impact of the strikes and the allegations that its warehouses supply the Russian military.

Russian entrepreneurs who use Wildberries for distribution have used social media to complain about the strikes and the devastating impact on their businesses.

“About 40% of our business went up in smoke,” said one fashion retailer in a post on Threads.

“Of course, compared to human lives, it is just money. The most important thing is that we and our loved ones are safe and sound. We had never stored such a large volume of products in marketplace (Wildberries) warehouses. However, due to new requirements, we had to urgently move the stock from our own warehouse, repackage it, and ship it to Wildberries.”

Another video that went viral on Ukrainian accounts featured a Russian retailer whose goods were at Wildberries warehouses in Krasnodar and Stavropol regions saying, “I just want this SMO (special military operation) to end.”

Russia’s largest online retailer Wildberries CEO Tatyana Kim attends the St. Petersburg International Economic Forum (SPIEF) on June 5. Olga Maltseva/AFP/Getty Images

Several Russian retailers complained that Wildberries’ terms of service had recently been changed to state that the e-retailer bears no liability for damage resulting from drone attacks.

In an interview posted by the business daily RBC, Wildberries founder Tatyana Kim said her company was discussing the possibility of tax relief and other measures with Russia authorities to aid sellers affected by attacks.

“We spoke with one of the agencies today – specifically, the Federal Tax Service – regarding the potential development of measures to ease the tax burden for affected entrepreneurs,” she said. “This isn’t about canceling taxes entirely, but rather about the possibility of granting deferrals or similar arrangements,” Kim said.

Ukrainian commentators, on the other hand, said the Wildberries complaints don’t explain the bigger picture: Russians, they say, ignore the fact that Moscow launched the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 that ultimately led to Ukraine’s campaign of deep strikes on Russia.

Kateryna Bohuslavska – who posts on X as “Kate from Kharkiv” – said, “Yet another flood of videos from Russians weeping over the ‘shock’ and ‘unfairness’ of strikes on a Wildberries warehouse. ​It doesn’t cross their minds how unfair it felt when we were just living our lives, bothering no one, in our own country and our own homes, right up until their missiles started tearing our cities apart on a chilly winter morning.”

A firefighting helicopter attempts to extinguish a fire at the Russian e-commerce firm Wildberries’ logistics complexes in the town of Elektrostal outside Moscow on July 18. Tatyana Makeyeva/AFP/Getty Images

Anton Gerashchenko, a Ukrainian social media influencer and former official, said Russians should point the finger of blame at Russian President Vladimir Putin.

“Russians found out their country is waging a war. The next step is for them to realize who is responsible for all the damage caused to Russia (Putin),” he wrote on X.

“Wildberries is no longer just an online marketplace for clothing and household goods. The platform sells weapons, body armor, drones, drone components, and fiber-optics used for drones. All of these items are used in the war against Ukraine and help kill Ukrainians. That is why such facilities are legitimate military targets for Ukraine’s Armed Forces.”

Russians are unlikely to direct public rage toward Putin, particularly in a country where dissent is not tolerated and criticism of the military is outlawed. But the Wildberries strikes are bringing home the war for Russians in a new way.

World.title: ‘Going it alone does not work’: America’s first one-party war
World.content:
As President Donald Trump pleads for tens of billions of dollars to pay for the nation’s war with Iran, Democrats in Congress have offered an unequivocal — and historically unusual — message.

No.

Trump’s operation in Iran has now become the most partisan war in modern US history, marking the first time that one party is willing to fully reject wartime funding requests from the country’s commander-in-chief.

Democrats are, for the first time in at least a century, in lockstep against a war from the start. They are refusing to support more funding. They are voting en masse to demand Trump pull troops out. They are even rejecting a broader Pentagon policy measure in protest — which includes provisions mostly unrelated to this particular war, such as one that would raise troop pay.

It’s a seismic political shift from years past, when Democrats would cower from accusations of not supporting troops in the middle of a conflict. But party lawmakers contend that the American public, including Republican voters, are on their side, and that the GOP’s support for the war will be a real dividing line heading into the November election.

“They absolutely own it,” a fired-up Rep. Pat Ryan of New York, who served two tours in Iraq, said of Republicans. “We’ve lost multiple additional soldiers. They’ve lied and covered up casualties. Like, what are you doing?”

GOP leaders are furious, with Speaker Mike Johnson calling it “shameful” for Democrats to refuse funding for the Pentagon, especially amid concerns about depleted munitions and as the administration has sought nearly $70 billion more in emergency cash to help pay for military operations in Iran.

“Democrats don’t want to play along,” Johnson said. “Why? Because they have a problem with the president, and they think they’re going to get a political advantage over this.”

Democrats’ opposition is multifold. The party is generally more skeptical now of foreign entanglements and much less sympathetic to Israel, the key US partner in Iran. But the party is even more suspicious of Trump — particularly compared to the last GOP administration in wartime — and are incensed at how he’s handled nearly every part of the war in Iran. And they’re emboldened by the president’s failure to sell the conflict to the public from the beginning, setting the table for a war that is uniquely unpopular just months into the conflict, despite fierce competition for that mantle.

‘Going it alone’

Led by their ranks of military veterans — like Ryan, who fought in the Middle East wars of the early 2000s — Democrats are now prepared to use their limited powers in the minority to block those funding requests until Trump and congressional Republicans can present a real plan to end the war.

And party leaders, like House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, plan to put those veterans at the centerpiece of their messaging going into the midterms, according to multiple sources briefed on those discussions.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries speaks to reporters after the House narrowly passed a resolution to halt US military action in Iran, at the US Capitol on July 23. J. Scott Applewhite/AP

“We’ve got to be willing to support the troops … but there are also times when we have to say enough is enough,” added Rep. Seth Moulton, a Marine Corps veteran who was deployed four times to Iraq.

“Clearly, with Trump and his losing war in Iran, Democratic veterans are saying enough is enough, and a lot of fellow Democrats are following our lead,” Moulton said.

As the US has stepped up its bombings in the last two weeks and the broader conflict escalates, the politics of the Iran war have become more perilous at home. Just 29% of Americans support it, according to a recent Washington Post-Ipsos poll, and even some Republicans acknowledge there’s been virtually no attempt to convince the public, or Congress, why the war is necessary.

Rep. Don Bacon, a Republican defense hawk who is retiring from politics this year, said Trump is to blame for failing to bring Democrats on board.

“I don’t think the president’s done a good job trying to get bipartisan support for this. Going it alone does not work,” warned Bacon, who spent 29 years in the Air Force, including as a commander in Iraq.

A protester interrupts Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth as he testifies at a hearing of the Senate Appropriations Committee, on July 21. Jacquelyn Martin/AP

In the five months since the first US airstrikes killed Iranian leaders, Trump and his Pentagon leaders have said little about their plans abroad, with highly mixed messages about the overall objectives. Even in private briefings, senior lawmakers have been unable to get answers to basic questions about the Pentagon’s funding needs or strategy.

“The idea that … ‘we don’t need a single Democrat,’ it’s not smart. Because in the end, we need these guys. We need to have a better defense for our country,” Bacon said.

Democrats project campaign confidence

In another mark of the dramatic political shift from after the last pair of Middle East wars, the House’s most endangered Democrats insist they aren’t worried about a barrage of GOP attacks for not supporting the troops.

“I’m sure they’ll campaign that way,” Rep. Henry Cuellar, who represents a competitive district in south Texas and sits on a critical defense spending subcommittee, said of the potential GOP attacks.

But, he added: “It’s very unpopular. People are tying it to the high gasoline prices. Part of it, (Trump) campaigned he was going to stop endless wars, and here we are.”

Rep. Susie Lee, who represents a swing seat in Nevada, made clear she would not support the GOP’s Iran funding plan — “I’m not voting for it” — and said her biggest priority is getting information for her own active-duty constituents who are under attack overseas.

“I’ve supported defense spending. I will continue to support spending and support our troops, but there’s no strategy on how this war is going to end,” she said.

For Republicans in difficult races, the issue can be complicated. They’re trying to align themselves with the military but also are fully aware of voter anger about higher prices at the pump.

“We have to protect America. We have to protect American troops,” said Sen. Jon Husted, a vulnerable Ohio Republican. “I want the war to end, I want the war to be over, I want gas prices to come down, but I also don’t want to weaken our military.”

Sen. Jon Husted speaks during a Senate Appropriations Committee hearing on President Donald Trump’s supplemental funding request for the Department of Defense, on July 21. Eric Lee/Reuters

Sen. Susan Collins, the endangered Maine moderate locked in a tough battle for reelection, was non-committal when asked if she’d back more funds, noting that her Senate Appropriations Committee had just heard testimony from Pentagon leaders about the funding request.

“Now the committee will work its will,” she said.

A very different Middle East war

In 2007, at the height of the insurgency in the Iraq war, then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi helped to deliver tens of billions of dollars for the Bush administration’s two increasingly unpopular wars in the Middle East.

Roughly two decades later, the former wartime speaker is clear that she will not vote to support Trump’s war in Iran in any fashion.

“It has not been approved by Congress. And we don’t see a plan, a purpose, an exit strategy. That’s the sloppiest approach to our national security that I’ve ever seen,” Pelosi told CNN.

Pelosi, a San Francisco liberal, had voted against authorizing Bush’s war with Iraq back in 2002. But roughly 40% of her fellow House Democrats did support it, as well as more than half of Senate Democrats, including Joe Biden, Hillary Clinton and then-Rep. Adam Schiff. That vote came after a furious pressure campaign by the Bush administration to sway lawmakers to back the operations, including public hearings, member briefings and speeches.

The push to support troops in warzones at that time was so strong that Democrats repeatedly acquiesced to the Bush administration’s funding requests — even after Pelosi and her party took back the House a year prior with pledges to bring troops home.

It wasn’t the first time Democrats had bowed to the pressure.

Rep. Emanuel Cleaver, a senior Democrat from Missouri, recalled watching as a child as then-President Richard Nixon spent years trying to sell the public on the war with Vietnam.

That sales pitch ultimately failed. But, Cleaver argued, Nixon and right-hand man Henry Kissinger at least would “come across as strategic.” Democrats in Congress continued to fund the war until the very end.

With Trump’s operations in Iran, however, there has been no vote to go to war. The president has made no argument to voters or to Congress.

‘Nobody likes it’

And there’s dwindling support even in Trump’s own party.

“I think 95% of everybody in that room in there realizes that this is a mistake, and there’s no way out,” Cleaver said, nodding toward the House chamber, where every Democrat — and a handful of Republicans — had just voted to halt Trump’s war in Iran.

On his way to the House chamber that day, Cleaver walked the halls with a Republican member, whom he refused to name but said privately ranted about the war.

“He was saying, ‘This is absolutely crazy.’ Nobody likes it. Even the guys who are gonna support the bill don’t want it.’ They realize that this is a quagmire,” Cleaver said.

An American flag flies at half-staff outside the home of the family of fallen US soldier Sgt. Angel S. Rampersad, who was killed during an Iranian attack in Jordan, in New York, on July 23. Jordan Tovin/Reuters

Sen. Rand Paul of Kentucky is one of the few Republicans who will say it out loud.

“The Iran war has not been a success. I’ve been opposed to the Iran war from the beginning,” Paul said. “I think, by any objective matter, we’re worse off, we’re measurably worse off than we were before the war.”

Asked if Republicans would suffer backlash at the polls come November, Paul deadpanned.

“Probably,” he said.

World.title: Amr Diab: Unlocking the secret of the trend
World.content:
With almost every new album release, Amr Diab faces a remarkably predictable wall of criticism—much of it filtered through a rigidly moralistic lens.

Yet Diab remains entirely unfazed by these judgments.

He lives every single day laser-focused on one goal: creating the next jaw-dropping release that forces all eyes and ears back onto him.

He makes no attempt to hide the fact that he is approaching 65. Instead, he operates with the conviction that his biological age is at least 25 years younger.

But that agelessness doesn’t come cheap – he pays a steep price for it. His gym sessions only lengthen as the years roll on, driven by the reality that physical fitness accounts for at least half of a performer’s staying power—after all, audiences listen with their eyes, too.

Diab keeps a sharp, relentless eye on emerging trends in both the global and local music scenes.

His personal doctrine is simple: never waste energy outside the realm of art.

Above all, he is fearless when it comes to taking risks. He knows that people—or at least the majority—instinctively push back against anything new or unconventional.

Yet, before long, that same audience adapts to the fresh sound, left wondering why it took them so long to embrace it in the first place.

Inevitably, Diab’s fanbase is split into two camps: the loyalists of his early era, and the post-2000s generation—his “new audience.”

The late legendary composer Mohamed Abdel Wahab once faced a similar dilemma, caught between purists who adored his early classics like “Ahwan Aleyk” and “Elli Yihebb El Gamal,” and fans who embraced his modern hits like “Ana Wel ‘Azab Wa Hawak” and “Ah Mennak Ya Garehni.”

While Abdel Wahab constantly tried to strike a middle ground to please both sides, Diab understands that in today’s era, reinvention is the key to survival.

He thereby chooses to lean entirely into the current cultural moment.

In his latest album, “Habbaitak”, Diab dives headfirst into the most current trends in songwriting and production. As a listener, you might find some of the lyrics and melodies disconcerting at first—and that is entirely by design.

Diab does nothing by accident.

Moustafa Hadouta, the undisputed king of Mahraganat lyricists who penned Hassan Shakosh’s breakout hit “Bint El Geeran”, has now become a permanent fixture in Diab’s creative circle.

On this record alone, Hadouta boasts three tracks—the most provocative on the album, and predictably, the ones drawing the most online criticism. Their collaboration began two years ago with “Ya Qamar” and continued with “Qafalti El Leaba”, but on this latest release, Hadouta pulled off a lyrical hat-trick with “Wa Enti Gambi”, “12 Bel Lail”, and “El Alwan”.

The latter two tracks, in particular, immediately set social media ablaze.

Diab undoubtedly knew they would invite wild interpretations, over-analysis, and moral outrage—so much so that the initial shock value turned them into prime material for internet memes and caricatures.

The 12-track album features a rich mix of composers, including Mohamed Yehia, Amr Mostafa, and Ehab Abdel Wahed, alongside a major comeback from Nader Nour.

It also introduces the project’s youngest talent—15-year-old Adham Ayman Bahgat Qamar—while drawing on lyricists like Amir Teima, Tamer Hussein, Menna El Kiey, Razam, Ayman Bahgat Qamar, and Moustafa El Prince. Notably, Diab himself composed the track “Lola El Banat.”

Diab’s composing talent is both innate and profound, yet he is far too shrewd to limit his catalog to his own melodies. He possesses a remarkably sharp ear, allowing him to hunt down and claim the absolute best work from others.

Never letting external distractions throw him off course, he has held the secret to staying consistently at the top for over forty years.

Author’s biography:

Tarek al-Shenawy is a journalist, film critic, and professor of film criticism at the Faculty of Mass Communication, Cairo University.

He holds a Bachelor’s degree from the Faculty of Mass Communication in Cairo University, and a Bachelor’s degree from the Institute of Cinema.

Shenawy has won numerous awards for best critical article from the Syndicate of Journalists multiple times, as well as from film societies. He was awarded the title of Best Popular Film Critic by the “Der Giest” Association in 2015 – a title that has not been awarded to anyone since.

He has also chaired and participated in the judging committees of numerous international film festivals, including the Valencia and Dubai Film Festivals.

He began practicing film criticism nearly 35 years ago in the Rose al-Yousse magazine and continues to write a weekly column titled “Kalma we Nos” (Word and a Half) on its pages. He has written for numerous magazines, newspapers, and websites both inside and outside Egypt.

He currently writes a daily column in Al-Masry Al-Youm newspaper and a weekly column in Al-Sharq al-Awsat newspaper, and has published over thirty books.

World.title: Video: Young swimmer rescues fainting competitor mid-race in Alexandria
World.content:
A young Egyptian swimmer saved his teammate’s life after the latter fainted during a 100-meter freestyle race.

During the qualifying rounds of the Alexandria Summer Swimming Championship, a swimmer lost consciousness in his lane.

Recognizing the danger, his teammate, Adam Mohamed Refaat—competing in the adjacent lane—acted instantly, swimming over to pull him out of the water in a rapid response that prevented the situation from worsening.

Once he was brought out of the pool, medical personnel and organizers intervened to administer the necessary first aid until his condition stabilized.

The courageous actions of the Raya Club athlete drew widespread praise from attendees, who called for him to be officially honored for his heroic act.

A previous tragedy

The incident brought back memories of the tragedy involving junior swimmer Youssef Mohamed, who drowned after losing consciousness during a race at the National Championship at Cairo Stadium last year.

Back in February, the Cairo Misdemeanor Court sentenced several defendants in the drowning case—including the chief referee and three rescue crew members—to three years in prison with a bail of LE 10,000 each.

The ruling also imposed a fine of LE 5,000 on the President of the Swimming Federation, members of its board of directors, the executive director, the head of the competitions committee, and the tournament director, following their conviction for negligence and dereliction of duty, while acquitting them of involuntary manslaughter charges.

World.title: West Bank raids result in death of Gaza police chief and arrest of 40 people in a single village
World.content:
The West Bank is now under siege from rapidly escalating Israeli settlement activity and military operations on Saturday, coinciding with mounting Arab and international condemnations of settler violence.

Settlers established a new settlement outpost north of Nablus, while Israeli occupation forces launched widespread raid and arrest campaigns targeting dozens of Palestinians across several governorates. Meanwhile, the United Nations, Jordan, and the Palestinian leadership called for holding settlers accountable and halting the ongoing attacks.

Several Palestinians on Saturday were killed and others injured in a series of strikes executed by Israeli aircraft across various parts of the Gaza Strip.

The Ministry of Interior in Gaza announced the death of the Director of North Gaza Governorate Police, Brigadier General Abdel Nasser Mohammad Al-Maqadma (54), following an Israeli airstrike targeting him in the Sheikh Radwan neighborhood, northwest of Gaza City.

The Al-Baidar Organization for the Defense of Bedouin Rights stated that the establishment of the new outpost is part of a plan aimed at fragmenting Palestinian areas and isolating vast tracts of agricultural land.

The organization warned that this will increase restrictions on Palestinian movement and double the pressure faced by local residents and farmers.

This coincided with a series of settler attacks across various regions of the West Bank.

Groups of settlers attacked the outskirts of the Jaba community and several Palestinian homes – the residents repelled the attack and forced the assailants to retreat without causing significant property damage.

The attacks extended to several villages and towns in the Nablus Governorate, where settlers under the protection of occupation forces raided agricultural lands and homes near settlements.

They also blocked roads and hurled stones at Palestinian vehicles as part of repeated attacks aimed at expanding land control and imposing further restrictions on the population.

Expanded military operations

Israeli occupation forces expanded their military operations in the West Bank, conducting a campaign of raids and arrests that covered Qalqilya, Nablus, Ramallah, Jenin, Hebron, Bethlehem, Tulkarm, Tubas, Jericho, and Jerusalem.

Palestinian sources told the WAFA news agency that occupation forces arrested at least 14 Palestinians in the Ramallah Governorate and around 40 others during a raid on the village of Till, southwest of Nablus.

The UN Special Rapporteur on the situation of human rights in the Palestinian territory occupied since 1967, Francesca Albanese, stated that Israeli settlers are “escalating their deadly attacks against defenseless Palestinians in the West Bank,” calling for those responsible to be held accountable.

She added that settlers shot Palestinians “in cold blood” in the towns of Till and Far’ata, emphasizing that the continuation of these attacks reflects the state of impunity enabled by the protection that occupation forces provide to the settlers.

The Jordanian Ministry of Foreign Affairs condemned the escalation of settler attacks, reaffirming its absolute rejection of the assaults targeting Palestinian villages.

Edited translation from Al-Masry Al-Youm

World.title: Egyptian, Saudi FMs discuss de-escalating regional tensions
World.content:
Minister of Foreign Affairs Badr Abdelatty discussed with Saudi Minister of Foreign Affairs Prince Faisal bin Farhan during a phone call on Saturday, July 25, 2026, regional and international efforts to de-escalate rising regional tensions.

The call falls within the framework of following up on the latest regional developments.

The ministers stressed the need to immediately halt military actions, prioritize diplomatic solutions and intensify Arab coordination to maintain regional stability.

They also agreed on safeguarding freedom of navigation under international law and rejecting attempts to obstruct international waterways.

World.title: OPINION: Nyon’go, Nyon’go Nyon’go: Has the ‘Mufasa Effect’ of the Two Boys Gotten Under HH’s Skin?
World.content:
Nyon’go, Nyon’go: Has the ‘Mufasa Effect’ of the Two Boys Gotten Under HH’s Skin?

By Mabvuto Banda

There are moments in an election campaign when a politician says far more through his temperament than through the actual words coming out of his mouth. President Hakainde Hichilema’s repeated “Nyon’go, Nyon’go, Nyon’go” utterances, directed at Gary Nkombo, may have been intended as political theatre, but they revealed something else: a President appearing increasingly willing to abandon presidential restraint and descend into the language of irritation and ridicule. The “Nyon’go” remarks were not directed at Brian Mundubile or Makebi Zulu, and that distinction matters. But so does the temperament behind them. At this stage of an increasingly competitive campaign, such an outburst inevitably raises questions about whether the pressure is beginning to show.

For a man who is not only Head of State but also an elder in the church, the tone was particularly striking. A President is entitled to campaign aggressively, defend his record and challenge his opponents, but there is a difference between campaigning hard and appearing to lose the dignity that comes with the office. The presidency does not disappear simply because there is a microphone, a rally and an opponent to attack. And perhaps that is where the real story lies. Something appears to be getting under the President’s skin.

The “Nyon’go” episode may have involved Nkombo, but elsewhere on the campaign trail, the two men Hichilema repeatedly dismisses as “boys” have brought something to this election that also seems to be testing his patience. The confidence remains, but increasingly, so does the irritation.

THE MUFASA EFFECT

It is becoming something of a Mufasa effect. In The Lion King, Mufasa’s name alone carried weight. Mention it in the wrong company and the reaction was immediate: fear, discomfort and a sudden change of mood. Mufasa did not even have to enter the room. Sometimes the name alone was enough.

That is increasingly what Brian Mundubile and Makebi Zulu appear to be doing to President Hichilema politically. These are the same two men he has repeatedly reduced to “boys”, yet listen to how much political attention they now command. The more dismissive the language becomes, the harder it is to believe that the people being dismissed are politically irrelevant. If the “boys” do not matter, why do they appear to provoke such a reaction?

That is the Mufasa effect. It is not necessarily about who is stronger or who will ultimately win on August 13. That decision belongs to the Zambian people. It is about the psychological effect an opponent begins to have on another. Right now, Mundubile and Zulu appear to have found a way of occupying political space that their supposed insignificance should never have allowed.

THEN CAME THE COPPERBELT

Then came the Copperbelt, where NRPUP campaign vehicles were reportedly attacked and their windows shattered by people the opposition identified as UPND cadres. A driver was allegedly assaulted, while cash and a mobile phone were reportedly stolen from the convoy. Later came the extraordinary scenes in Luanshya, where Mundubile’s convoy encountered a police blockade as it attempted to reach supporters waiting in Mpatamatu.

And that begs an even bigger question: what peace is President Hakainde Hichilema actually talking about? On the ground in Mpatamatu on Friday, peace looked like this: an opposition convoy pelted with stones, a road into Luanshya sealed off by the very police force that is supposed to protect every candidate equally, and a presidential hopeful forced to talk his way past a blockade simply to reach voters who had been waiting for him.

If this is what the President’s “peace” produces, it is worth asking who it is actually peaceful for, because it was certainly not peaceful for Mundubile’s campaign. Vehicles were stoned. Police blocked the road. And this was not an isolated incident. On the same day, NRPUP campaign vehicles elsewhere on the Copperbelt reportedly had their windows smashed, a driver assaulted, and cash and a phone stolen.

Mundubile said his people had been attacked, assaulted and their vehicles vandalised while the government continued to speak of a peaceful campaign season. That description of peace is becoming increasingly difficult to reconcile with what Zambians are seeing.

KALINGALINGA CANNOT BE ERASED

And Luanshya did not happen in a vacuum. Only a week earlier came Kalingalinga, where police used teargas during a confrontation surrounding an opposition campaign event and reports emerged that a young girl had been shot. Government officials subsequently disputed aspects of the account, maintaining that police had used teargas and that no lives were lost. Whatever version one accepts, Kalingalinga raised uncomfortable questions about the policing of opposition political activities during an already heated election campaign.

Then, on the same afternoon as the Luanshya blockade, police walked onto Mundubile’s campaign stage in Ndola. By the time his convoy encountered trouble in Luanshya, interaction with law enforcement was becoming part of the opposition’s campaign story rather than something happening at its margins. Kalingalinga, Ndola and Luanshya have different circumstances and must each be judged on their own facts, but taken together with the reported attacks on campaign vehicles, they leave an uncomfortable question about the environment in which the opposition is being expected to campaign.

THE DISCIPLINE OF THE ‘TWO BOYS’

What is remarkable is not simply that stones reportedly flew or that police blocked a road being used by a presidential candidate. What is remarkable is that Mundubile and his running mate Makebi Zulu refused to give the provocation the reaction it appeared capable of producing. They did not turn the convoy around. They did not allow shattered windows, stones or a police blockade to become bigger than the political message they had travelled to deliver.

They proceeded to Mpatamatu and addressed the people who had been waiting for them. Zulu stood before miners, youths and farmers and told them in Bemba that their cries had been heard. Mundubile, rather than spending his speech attacking those accused of trying to prevent him from reaching the rally, pledged to establish a National Miners’ Day to honour the men and women whose labour has helped build Zambia’s economy.

That is discipline, but it is also political calculation. The opposition appears to understand that one angry reaction could change the entire story. A scuffle, a retaliatory stone, a broken window or an exchange with police could quickly provide the excuse to stop a procession, disrupt a rally or portray the opposition itself as the source of disorder.

The opposition therefore finds itself carrying an extraordinary burden. It must campaign, absorb provocation and simultaneously police its own reaction. It must remain calm enough not only to protect its supporters, but also to deny those confronting it the very excuse that could be used to restrict its campaign further.

WHAT PEACE ARE WE TALKING ABOUT?

That is why the President’s own temperament matters. “Nyon’go, Nyon’go, Nyon’go” was directed at Gary Nkombo, not Mundubile or Zulu. But the episode remains relevant because it offered a glimpse of a President appearing increasingly impatient at precisely the moment when Zambia needs presidential restraint most.

When the same Head of State is also reducing political opponents to “boys”, while opposition vehicles are reportedly being damaged and opposition convoys are encountering police blockades, the contrast becomes difficult to ignore. The President may regard some of this language as campaign banter, but presidential words carry a weight that ordinary campaign rhetoric does not. The office requires more.

President Hichilema cannot demand peaceful conduct from everyone beneath him while creating the impression that political pressure is eroding his own patience. He cannot preach restraint while allowing his language to drift towards ridicule. And those entrusted with maintaining law and order cannot allow circumstances to develop in which opposition candidates appear to require extraordinary patience simply to exercise their right to campaign.

The burden of maintaining peace cannot rest on the opposition simply refusing to retaliate. Real peace is not achieved when one side throws a stone and the other side decides not to throw it back. Real peace exists when nobody is allowed to throw the stone in the first place, and when the police stand between competing political forces without fear, favour or partisan appearance.

WHEN THE REACTION SAYS IT ALL

This is where the Mufasa effect becomes politically interesting. Nobody needs to pretend that Mundubile and Zulu have already won anything. Zambians will make that decision themselves on August 13. President Hichilema remains the incumbent and continues to campaign on his government’s record. Elections are decided by voters, not metaphors.

But you do not need to win an election before you begin affecting the behaviour of your opponent. Sometimes you simply need to get into his head. Perhaps the “boys” have brought more to the table than was anticipated. Perhaps Mundubile and Zulu have discovered that refusing to be provoked can itself become a political weapon.

Perhaps the scenes from Kalingalinga to the Copperbelt matter precisely because they allow voters to compare the temperament of those wielding power with the restraint of those seeking it. Government officials have denied wrongdoing in relation to previous incidents, while responsibility for the reported Copperbelt attacks must ultimately be established through proper investigation rather than political accusation. Police had offered no comment on Friday’s reported convoy attack at the time of writing.

But politically, the images already carry their own weight. Zambians vote on August 13. The closer that date gets, the less useful speeches about peace become if the experience on the ground tells another story. Kalingalinga happened. Then came Ndola, the reported attacks on campaign vehicles and the confrontation in Luanshya. Against that background stands a President whose language appears increasingly impatient as the “two boys” he has repeatedly dismissed refuse to disappear.

“Nyon’go, Nyon’go, Nyon’go” was directed at Gary Nkombo, but perhaps its wider significance was the glimpse it offered of a President under pressure. And that is what makes the Mufasa effect interesting.

Mundubile and Zulu do not have to say they are getting under the President’s skin. Sometimes, the reaction says it for them.

World.title: Safeguard the country’s peace-HH
World.content:
President Hakainde Hichilema has urged more than 5,000 young Zambians to safeguard the country’s peace ahead of the upcoming election, warning that violence and instability can strip away everything a nation has built.

Hichilema made the appeal while addressing the Seventh-day Adventist Church’s Youth Conference Big Sabbath at Blessing Centre in Lusaka, taking a break from a week of back-to-back campaign rallies in Southern Province to attend the gathering.

“Without peace, everything is gone. Literally everything is gone,” the President said, delivering what he described as a reflective, off-the-cuff message on the importance of preserving peace.

He pointed to the Democratic Republic of Congo, which has struggled to achieve lasting peace for decades, as an illustration of the consequences of prolonged instability, particularly for children who grow up surrounded by conflict.

“Just imagine raising a child in an environment of bullets and blood, from pregnancy to birth. Think of how the mother survives, the challenges during pregnancy, and the child who is born and is supposed to go to school at five, six or seven, but has no opportunity,” Hichilema said.

“What do you think they become when they are 20 or 25? They are fighting for survival. Do not wait to fight. We should cherish peace in our country.”

The Head of State thanked the young people for dedicating their gathering to peace at a politically important moment and urged them to continue bringing the nation together in prayer.

“I believe other young people will take a cue from what you are doing, what you have done today and what you are preaching,” he said.

Hichilema said he had been “extremely delighted” by the invitation and had chosen to travel to Lusaka specifically to attend the conference, despite initially not planning to be in the capital that morning.

“I knew that I would not be in Lusaka, but travelling here this morning to be part of the Lusaka Conference was a no-brainer,” he said.

In his homily, delivered under the theme “Driven by prayer, moved by faith” and drawn from 2 Chronicles 7:1-3 and 14, Pastor Heighten Hamweene urged the youth to emulate the biblical King Solomon, whose prayer was answered and whose land was healed.

Hamweene said God would likewise heal the nation if its people remained faithful and prayerful, reinforcing the conference’s message of peace, faith and national unity.

Southern Zambia Union Conference president Vanny Munyumbwe thanked Hichilema and his government for efforts to improve the welfare of Zambians, citing expanded access to education, strengthened community development, infrastructure investment and the promotion of peace and stability.

“As a church deeply involved in education, health care and community service, we value these efforts,” Munyumbwe said. “The SDA Church is part of the Government’s movement to contribute to human dignity and national development.”

The event featured a cappella music, scripture readings and a homily, with Hichilema, himself an elder in the Seventh-day Adventist Church, joining the congregation throughout the programme.

Before departing, the President donated a bus to the church grouping.

Hichilema’s remarks continued the peace message he has carried during the campaign period, having also conveyed similar appeals to other gatherings, including a message relayed to the Mutomboko traditional ceremony in Luapula Province.

The gathering came at a crucial stage of the election campaign, with young people forming a major part of the electorate and religious gatherings providing an avenue for reinforcing tolerance, peaceful participation and civic responsibility among young and first-time voters.

The President’s appeal also comes amid rising political tensions in parts of the country, with police confirming dozens of arrests linked to political violence on the Copperbelt this week. The incidents have added urgency to calls for restraint as Zambia enters the final stretch of campaigning ahead of the election.

World.title: Police arrest 27 as political violence flares on the Copperbelt
World.content:
Police have arrested 27 people, drawn from both the ruling and opposition camps, following incidents of political violence in Copperbelt and Central Province townships.

The unrest comes as campaigning for the general election enters its final and most volatile stretch.

Police public relations officer Godfrey Chilabi said 14 suspects, aligned to the Tonse Alliance and the National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity, were arrested after violence broke out during unauthorised roadshows in Chifubu and Kawama townships.

A separate group of 13 suspected United Party for National Development supporters was arrested and charged with disorderly conduct in Twapia Township on the same day.

Chilabi said the Tonse Alliance had properly notified police of planned presidential rallies in Kafulafuta and Twapia. Some supporters, however, went on to hold unapproved roadshows through Chifubu and Kawama.

When officers moved in to enforce compliance, a section of the crowd turned violent and threw stones at police.

“Tonse Alliance had notified police of its planned presidential campaign rallies in Kafulafuta and Twapia, but some supporters later conducted roadshows in Chifubu and Kawama townships without prior notice.”

“When police officers moved in to ensure compliance with the law, some supporters became violent and threw stones at the police,” Chilabi said.

The 14 suspects were formally charged with unlawful procession and have since been released on police bond.

In the separate Twapia incident, the 13 UPND supporters were detained, formally charged with disorderly conduct, and paid admission-of-guilt fines before being released.

Twapia Police Station also received a report the same day of a break-in and theft at the UPND secretariat offices at Twapia Old Market.

The report was filed by Henry Kabwebwe, 39, an aspiring UPND councillor for the ward, who said unknown persons forcibly entered the offices and stole two motorcycles and four bicycles.

Their combined value has not yet been established, and investigations continue.

Kitwe Central Police Station recorded seven separate reports of malicious damage to property believed to be politically motivated.

Chilabi said the damaged vehicles belonged to, or were being used by, NRPUP officials and supporters. Five of the incidents occurred at Sherbourne Hotel, while two others happened along Boma Street and near Mukuba Mall.

Seven dockets for malicious damage to property have been opened. Officers visited and processed the affected scenes before launching formal investigations.

“A task force has been constituted to thoroughly investigate the matter and ensure that all persons involved in the criminal acts are identified and brought to justice,” Chilabi said.

He appealed to the public to reject electoral violence, provocation, hate speech and misinformation that could undermine a peaceful vote.

“All organisers of political activities are urged to adhere to the campaign time-table issued by the Electoral Commission of Zambia and to conduct their activities peacefully, with respect for the rights of others,” he said.

This week’s arrests are the latest in a series of campaign-related flashpoints reported on the Copperbelt, a province regarded as pivotal to the outcome of the vote given its dense urban electorate and history of closely contested results.

Operation Young Vote executive director Isaac Mwale said elections are judged not only by what happens on the day people cast their ballots, but by how institutions, political actors, the media and citizens conduct themselves throughout the campaign period.

“Public confidence can be strengthened or undermined by stakeholder actions,” Mwale said.

He added that his organisation’s review of the campaign environment showed the process remained broadly on track despite isolated incidents.

The Electoral Commission of Zambia’s code of conduct requires parties to notify police of planned processions and rallies in advance, and obliges supporters to refrain from violence, property damage or provocation.

This week’s incidents illustrate the strain that enforcement of that code is coming under as candidates enter the final stretch of the race. The newly formed task force now faces pressure to secure prosecutions quickly enough to deter further confrontations before voters head to the polls.

World.title: Traditional leaders in Chembe laud government
World.content:
Traditional leaders in Chembe District of Luapula Province have praised the government for implementing development policies aimed at improving the livelihoods of local people.

Speaking when Vice President Mutale Nalumango visited the district, Chief Kasomalwela commended the government for increasing the enhanced Constituency Development Fund, saying the initiative has enabled the implementation of several development projects in the area.

Chief also welcomed the ongoing upgrade of the Pedicle Road, saying the project will ease the movement of goods and services and boost trade between Zambia and the neighboring Democratic Republic of Congo once completed.

However, he appealed to the government to ensure that the contractor, Sable Transport and Construction Limited, expedites works on the 11-kilometer stretch of the road.

Chief Kasomalwela further urged the government to rehabilitate the district’s feeder roads, which he said are in a poor state.

He also expressed satisfaction with the peaceful conduct of political campaigns ahead of the general elections.

Meanwhile, Chief Kalasalukangaba reiterated the call for the Pedicle Road project to be completed.

In her remarks, Vice President Mutale Nalumango emphasised the importance of collaboration between the government and traditional leaders, describing them as key partners in national development.

Mrs Nalumango acknowledged the concerns raised by the traditional leaders and urged the local authority to effectively utilise available earth-moving equipment to improve feeder roads in the district.

The Vice President also met members of the clergy, who appealed to the government to recruit more education and health personnel from within Chembe District.

Pastors Fellowship Chairperson, Leo Nkonde, said the church remains committed to promoting peaceful elections across the country.

Meanwhile, the Vice President called on the Church to continue praying for those in authority and the nation at large for peace and unity.

And, in a meeting with civil servants, Mrs Nalumango urged them to effectively understand and implement government policies.

Later, during a public meeting, Vice President Nalumango urged Chembe residents to vote for the UPND in the forthcoming general elections to sustain the country’s development agenda.

World.title: School Feeding Programme in Masaiti boosts education sector
World.content:
The School Feeding Programme in Masaiti District on the Copperbelt Province is transforming the education sector, with schools recording increased learner attendance and improved retention.

‎

‎Speaking in an interview with the media, Chamunda Primary School Headteacher, Mubita Lubala, said the programme has not only increased school attendance but has also improved learners’ concentration and active participation during lessons.

‎

‎Mr Lubala described the initiative as a timely intervention that has created a more conducive learning environment, especially for learners who had previously stopped attending school due to hunger and other challenges.

‎

‎He commended the government for prioritising the welfare of school-going children through the programme, noting that well-nourished learners are better positioned to perform well academically.

‎

‎Meanwhile, members of the community said the School Feeding Programme has encouraged more children to attend school consistently by providing daily meals while easing the burden on vulnerable households struggling to feed their children.

‎

‎One of the parents, Maggie Mavu, praised government for the initiative, saying it has helped address hunger among learners and motivated many children to attend school regularly because they are assured of receiving a meal while at school.

‎

‎Another parent, Miniver Katontomeka, said many children had previously stayed away from school due to lack of food, while others suffered from malnutrition.

‎

‎She noted that the introduction of the programme in schools has seen many learners return to school, giving them renewed hope for a better future through education.

‎

‎The community has since appealed to the government to sustain and expand the School Feeding Programme to more schools, saying the initiative remains key to improving education outcomes and ensuring that no child is left behind.

World.title: Govt. allocates K53 million towards Milk Pilot Programme in schools
World.content:
Government has allocated K53 Million towards the purchase and distribution of milk in 40 schools across the country under the Milk Pilot Programme.

The move is aimed at improving learner nutrition under the School Feeding Programme.

Ministry of Education Permanent Secretary for Administration, Noriana Muneku, says the milk programme is currently being implemented in four districts in each of the 10 provinces.

Ms Muneku said this in a speech read for her by Ministry of Education Director for Primary Education, Felix Ngoma, during the handover ceremony of a donation of five containers of food supplies from the Zambian Helpers Society and Korean Donor Company Limited to Lukamantano Secondary and Primary School in Chilanga District.

Ms Muneku explained that the initiative forms part of broader efforts to enhance the nutritional value of meals under the School Feeding Programme.

“As part of ongoing efforts to improve the nutritional value of school meals, the Ministry has also introduced a pilot programme of providing eggs to learners in Kabwe,” Ms Muneku said.

And Zambian Ambassador to South Korea, Andrew Banda, said the government values partnerships with organisations such as the Zambian Helpers Society that recognises education as a foundation for national development.

Mr Banda noted that contributions to the School Feeding Programme help strengthen government’s efforts and investment in learners for a better future.

Chilanga District Education Board Secretary, Lenny Longwe, expressed gratitude to the Zambian Helpers Society and Korean Donor Company for the timely donation, saying it will improve learner outcomes.

Dr Longwe added that the supplies will be utilised responsibly and for the intended purpose, in accordance with the government systems and accountability measures.

World.title: Over 800 Adults Return to School Under Free Education Programme in Kaoma
World.content:
Kaoma, Western Province – More than 800 adults in Kaoma District have returned to school through the government’s Youth and Adult Literacy Education (YALE) programme, which is being implemented under the free education policy.

Kaoma District Education Standards Officer for Open and Distance Learning, Ellen Ngombo, revealed that 882 adult learners from 50 centres across the district are currently enrolled in the programme. The learners, comprising both men and women, are acquiring literacy and numeracy skills as well as practical life skills such as agriculture, carpentry and tailoring.

Speaking during the commemoration of International Literacy Day at Kaoma Trades Training Institute, Ms Ngombo praised the learners for their commitment to education despite their age and encouraged them to inspire others to take advantage of the programme.

The event was held under the theme, “Literacy for People, Planet and Prosperity.”

Ms Ngombo said the programme has transformed the lives of many participants by equipping them with essential skills that enable them to improve their livelihoods.

“Today we have seen adult learners who can read, write and perform basic calculations. We have also seen learners who can use information and communication technology, keep business records and create products using the skills they have acquired,” she said.

“You are living proof that literacy changes lives, and we are proud of your achievements. Currently, 50 centres in the district are offering this programme, with 622 women and 260 men enrolled.”

Kaoma District Commissioner Kashina Sheba reaffirmed the government’s commitment to expanding access to literacy and skills development opportunities for individuals who missed out on formal education earlier in life.

Ms Sheba encouraged the learners to further their education by enrolling at Kaoma Trades Training Institute and the Youth Resource Centre, adding that government bursaries are available through the enhanced Constituency Development Fund (CDF).

“The main purpose of this event is to promote basic and functional literacy among young people and adult learners. I am impressed by what I have seen and heard from our learners today,” she said.

“You can also apply for CDF bursaries and continue developing your skills through training programmes offered at Kaoma Trades Training Institute and the Youth Resource Centre.”

Among the beneficiaries of the programme is 28-year-old Abigail Mulenga, a Grade Seven learner at Chilombo Primary School, who expressed gratitude to the government for providing her with a second chance at education.

Ms Mulenga said she is determined to complete her studies and build a better future for herself.

Another learner, Muhau Muleyabai from Mahilo Primary School, also commended the government for introducing the programme, noting that it has significantly improved her reading, writing and communication skills.

She added that the knowledge she has gained has helped her manage her business more effectively and confidently.

The YALE programme continues to provide a pathway for adults and youths who missed formal schooling, empowering them with literacy, numeracy and practical skills needed to improve their socio-economic well-being.
