According to her, wages for these positions have risen by a larger percentage than salaries for many higher-skilled professions, including finance specialists and translators.

Working conditions are more attractive at foreign companies

Ilona Khachatryan is a logistics specialist. She now works for an American company and earns four times more than she did two years ago in the same role at a local firm. But salary is only part of the reason she left. She says unhealthy relations with management at her former company also played a major role. More broadly, she is critical of hiring practices and personnel management at many local organisations.

“At the company where I worked, it was extremely difficult to receive the bonuses that management itself had promised. To avoid paying them, they would even falsify hourly timesheets.

I applied for jobs at other local companies as well. I attended interviews and then waited for months without hearing back. Even if they decide not to hire you, shouldn’t they at least tell you? After all, you invest your time and effort preparing for those interviews. Foreign companies treat candidates much more fairly. They make transparent hiring decisions. If they decide not to hire someone, they explain in detail why they cannot move forward with the candidate.”

Ilona says her current employer hired her after the first interview. The company immediately explained the salary, holiday entitlement, employment rights and job responsibilities.

“Hearing the words ‘thank you for your work’ genuinely motivates me. It gives me energy and makes me work with greater enthusiasm and commitment. And when your employer also recognises your achievements, you realise just how undervalued professionals are in the local labour market.”

Analysis of labour market trends in Armenia

World.title: Azerbaijan changes status of internally displaced people: What do new rules provide?
World.content:
The status of internally displaced persons in Azerbaijan

On 23 July, Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev signed into law amendments to the Law on the Status of Refugees and Internally Displaced Persons and the Law on the Social Protection of Internally Displaced Persons and Persons Equated with Them.

The amendments to the Housing Code provide for the creation of a Permanent Resettlement Fund in the territories liberated from occupation. Housing from the fund will be used to resettle internally displaced persons (IDPs) to the reclaimed territories and will later be transferred to them as private property.

The legislation also clarifies the grounds on which a person may lose IDP status. This applies to those who refuse housing offered by the state, as well as to those who are provided with alternative housing that meets the officially established housing standard for the relevant region instead of accommodation in their previous place of residence. At the same time, social protection measures will remain in place for three years after a person loses or voluntarily relinquishes their IDP status.

The changes are intended to strengthen the legal framework for the Great Return programme. In practice, however, they could significantly affect the lives of hundreds of thousands of people who have spent decades building their lives in Baku and other parts of Azerbaijan.

The purpose of the law and the benefits linked to IDP status

Under the previous legislation, internally displaced person (IDP) status entitled holders to a range of social benefits, including a monthly allowance of 60 manats (about $35) for each family member, state-funded tuition at fee-paying departments of public universities, and exemptions from certain government fees and utility payments.

For people forced to flee their homes in the early 1990s and who had spent decades living in dormitories, temporary housing units or other makeshift accommodation, these benefits represented a basic form of social support. The status also carried legal significance, as it formally recognised that they had been displaced against their will.

Under the new rules, the state is deemed to have fulfilled its obligations once it offers an internally displaced person permanent housing. If the person accepts the apartment, ownership is transferred to them, but they simultaneously lose their IDP status. Those who refuse the offer also lose their status and may forfeit the temporary accommodation provided to them in Baku or another city.

During a three-year transition period, only social support measures, including financial assistance and education benefits, will remain in place. The legal status itself, along with the other rights and guarantees associated with it, will cease to apply.

Freedom of choice and the problem of “any available housing”

The law refers to “alternative housing that complies with the standards established for the region of residence”. In practice, this means that internally displaced people are not necessarily offered housing in their native village or on their ancestral land.

For example, a person who owned several hectares of farmland before being displaced may now be offered a house in a newly built settlement with a plot of only 100–200 square metres. Ownership of their original land is not restored, as the state provides housing only. As a result, the concept of “returning home” is significantly narrowed.

According to dozens of families whose accounts have been shared on social media and in public appeals, many of the homes offered to them suffer from poor construction. They report leaking roofs during rainfall, flooded yards, and repeated disruptions to gas, water and electricity supplies. In some cases, applicants say they have been told verbally: “You’ve been given a house — be grateful, or you’ll lose that too.”

Similar complaints have also been submitted through official grievance mechanisms, although the issue has yet to generate wider public debate.

Life in Baku after three decades of integration

A large proportion of Azerbaijan’s internally displaced people have spent more than 30 years living in Baku and other major economic centres. Over that time, they have found employment, received an education, gained access to healthcare and established stable social networks. After losing their homes in the early 1990s, they were provided with temporary accommodation by the state, including places in dormitories, unfinished buildings and container settlements, as well as apartments in purpose-built residential complexes.

Under the new rules, however, this housing may be reclaimed once a person loses IDP status. As a result, many people face a difficult choice: accept an apartment in Karabakh and leave behind the life they have built in Baku, or lose both their IDP status and the accommodation provided to them by the state.

International human rights standards, including the UN Guiding Principles on Internal Displacement, require that return be voluntary, safe and carried out in dignity. These principles are based on freedom of choice, the provision of adequate housing and, wherever possible, the restoration of rights to former property. Under Azerbaijan’s new legislation, however, the state is considered to have fulfilled its obligations once it offers housing, while refusing that offer results in the loss of IDP status. This weakens the principle that return should be voluntary.

Official position and expert assessments

Pro-government media outlets, including Milli.az, Report.az and APA, have presented the amendments in a positive light, using phrases such as “restoring property rights”, “sustainable social support” and “providing a legal framework for the Great Return programme”.

MP Vugar Bayramov has also argued that the three-year transition period demonstrates the state’s continued commitment to social support. Official statements emphasise that the new housing is transferred into private ownership rather than provided on a rental basis, which the authorities say will encourage people to settle permanently in the region.

At the same time, independent observers and some human rights advocates argue that the changes restrict freedom of choice, fail to fully restore land rights and raise other concerns. They also point to the contrast between the urban lifestyles that many IDPs have built over the past three decades and the newly established rural settlements, as well as the risks of unemployment and inadequate infrastructure.

The status of internally displaced persons in Azerbaijan

World.title: EU’s 21st sanctions package targets Kulevi oil terminal and cryptocurrency platforms in Georgia
World.content:
Georgia in the EU’s 21st sanctions package

The European Union’s 21st package of sanctions against Russia includes an oil refinery in the Georgian town of Kulevi and several cryptocurrency platforms.

The sanctions against the Kulevi refinery, which processes and sells Russian oil, include a six-month grace period. The ban on transactions will take effect after six months unless the refinery changes its business practices.

The Kulevi refinery had previously been considered for inclusion in the EU’s 20th package of sanctions against Russia, but was ultimately removed from the sanctions list.

At the time, the EU said that “the Georgian authorities and the port operator had made positive commitments.” This was stated in a letter from the EU’s Special Envoy, David O’Sullivan, to Georgian Foreign Minister Maka Botchorishvili.

What does the new sanctions package include?

The EU’s 21st package of sanctions against Russia, which is expected to take effect shortly, was formally approved by the permanent representatives of the EU member states on 23 July 2026.

The sanctions are expected to enter into force on 23 July following approval by EU leaders and their publication in the Official Journal of the European Union.

The measures target sectors of the Russian economy that generate significant revenue for Moscow’s war in Ukraine, including energy, financial services and the cryptocurrency sector.

The package also imposes sanctions on more than 50 companies and organisations involved in supplying military goods and weapons to Russia.

It includes the EU’s largest-ever round of individual sanctions, targeting a total of 218 entities — 48 individuals and 170 legal entities.

It is one of the most significant expansions of the EU’s sanctions regime in the past four years.

Sanctions against the Kulevi refinery

“The package introduces the possibility of banning transactions with oil refineries listed in Russia and third countries that process Russian crude oil and petroleum products. Under these measures, the EU is imposing a ban on transactions with the Georgian oil refinery in Kulevi, which processes and trades Russian oil. The ban will take effect in six months,” the EU said in a statement.

According to Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty, citing a source familiar with the matter, the introduction of a six-month deadline is unprecedented in EU sanctions policy.

The same source said the decision reflected Tbilisi’s willingness to meet the EU’s requirements, which became apparent during discussions over sanctions related to the port.

This means that if the Kulevi refinery continues processing Russian oil over the next six months, it will become subject to EU sanctions. The refinery’s owner, Black Sea Petroleum, announced on 1 July 2026 that it would begin full-scale processing of non-Russian crude from August or September.

According to Georgia’s National Statistics Office, domestic exports rose sharply in January 2026 compared with the same period a year earlier, driven largely by exports of petroleum products.

Petroleum and petroleum products ranked as Georgia’s second-largest export category in January 2026, with exports worth $58.7 million, accounting for 12.2% of the country’s total exports.

Cryptocurrency platforms added to the sanctions list

The EU has imposed transaction bans on 14 cryptocurrency platforms based in Georgia, Panama, the United Arab Emirates, Kyrgyzstan, Belarus and the Marshall Islands.

For the first time, the EU has introduced a mechanism allowing it to impose a complete ban on transactions between EU companies and cryptocurrency platforms that help Russia circumvent sanctions.

The measure also applies to crypto service providers operating in third countries if they facilitate activities that serve Russian interests.

What does the inclusion of Georgian companies in the sanctions package mean for Georgia?

The inclusion of the Kulevi refinery in the EU’s 21st sanctions package has already sparked debate in Georgia.

“The EU’s 21st sanctions package is a national disgrace: Georgian assets are being used as cannon fodder for Russia’s war machine. By allowing the Kremlin to circumvent sanctions, those in power are betraying our sovereignty. Georgia’s place is in Europe — we will never become a loophole for Russian aggression,” Georgia’s fifth president, Salome Zourabichvili, wrote on X.

Analyst Lela Djedjelava said sanctions against such an important economic asset would have an impact on the Georgian economy.

“The consequences will become increasingly visible over time. The reality is that the Kulevi refinery is probably not the only facility that could be exposed for cooperating with Russia. If other businesses in Georgia are also hit by sanctions, it will naturally have a very negative impact on the country.”

Gedevan Popkhadze, one of the leaders of the opposition Coalition for Change, said the EU sanctions against the Kulevi refinery were the result of the Georgian government’s inaction.

“If you are not helping Ukraine, why are you helping Russia? If you do not want war, why are you acting in favour of one of the parties to the conflict? We must clearly understand that these sanctions are not a message to the Kulevi refinery itself — they are a message to Georgia’s de facto government. It should realise that claiming to be neutral is hypocrisy.”

Georgia in the EU’s 21st sanctions package

World.title: Diamonds disappointed Glasgow games only live on Seven's streaming service
World.content:
The Diamonds are one of the most successful and beloved teams in Australian sport, but some fans back home trying to tune in to their Commonwealth Games campaign have been left disappointed.

The reigning netball gold medallists kicked off with dominant wins by a combined 80 goals on Saturday and Sunday, but neither match was carried live on any of Seven Network's linear television channels.

The 99-38 victory over Tonga and 66-47 win over England were only shown live on streaming service 7Plus, while Seven carried the swimming heats.

For Sunday's prime-time match against rivals and 2018 champions the Roses, Seven aired 2021 Ryan Reynolds film Free Guy on Mate, and crime drama Vera on TWO.

The Diamonds' Glasgow games have been carried live on 7Plus, but not on Seven's linear TV channels. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Seven's main channel broadcast made clear the Diamonds were live on Plus.

After the swimming finished and the Diamonds had won, the Australia-England game was aired on delay on Seven's main channel.

ABC Sport broke the news to a few of the Diamonds stars after their game.

"That's obviously disappointing, obviously we want to be on TV and have every fan able to watch. I wasn't aware of that," goalkeeper Courtney Bruce said.

"I don't know, hopefully we'll be able to be on the live games [at some point]. It is disappointing, we obviously want netball to be highlighted and want the rest of the sports here at the Commonwealth Games and for Australia to be highlighted too."

Games debutant Jamie-Lee Price said she hopes fans keep making their voices heard.

Sunday's game was between the last two Commonwealth gold medallists. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

"I think maybe if we put lots of pressure on maybe we can get there," she said.

"I didn't realise that. We want to be on TV, we want eyes on our sport and if we can get that that's amazing. So, yes please."

The silver lining of the situation is the reminder of the support this team has in Australia and in Glasgow, where the Australians in the Hydro were challenging the English fans for sheer volume and passion.

"We definitely feel the support from home, obviously we're nothing without the supporters back in Australia," Bruce said.

The Diamonds' next match is against Malawi in two days' time. (Getty Images: Rob Casey/SNS Group)

"We definitely feel it today and there's quite a few out there. That was really nice to have them out there today."

A Channel Seven spokesperson responded to requests from the ABC, saying:

"The Glasgow 2026 Commonwealth Games features multiple events taking place simultaneously, which is why Seven is delivering wall-to-wall coverage across Seven and 7plus Sport — including 15 live channels on 7plus Sport — ensuring Australians can watch every event live and free."

World.title: Piastri blasts '**** stupid' backmarker, Norris wins Hungarian GP
World.content:
Oscar Piastri was forced to retire from the Formula 1 Hungarian Grand Prix, but not before he blasted a "stupid" backmarker and slammed his team for a poor strategy at the Hungaroring.

Lando Norris claimed his first victory of the season, ahead of Max Verstappen in second and world championship leader Kimi Antonelli in third.

Piastri was left desperately frustrated after a brilliant start saw him overtake his teammate on the opening lap to take the lead from third on the grid.

"It was definitely the highlight of my race," Piastri said of the start.

"And it went pretty downhill from there.

"A lot of things to unpack."

The Australian leaped into the lead but never was able to pull away, complaining of rear tyre wear as Norris was all over the back of his teammate in a clearly faster car.

"The pace on the hard tyres was nowhere," Piastri bemoaned.

At the half-way point, when he was brought into the pits for his second stop in response to Lewis Hamilton doing so.

McLaren, wary of the under-cut, had been pestered by Norris to allow him to pit first and had even told him to box on lap 32, saying he was "miles" faster than Piastri, but the team said the reigning world champion was unable to come in as Piastri had first choice on the pit stop.

Oscar Piastri leads Lando Norris. (Getty Images" Andy Hone/LAT Images)

Piastri did come in, but was then caught behind back markers and, as he tried to complete his outlaps was hit by Carlos Sainz as he battled with the Aston Martin.

"Is he **** stupid or what? Get out of the **** way, you idiot! Oh my god," Piastri said as Sainz first held him up, then clipped his front wheel.

Piastri's mood did not improve soon after when Norris, having stayed out longer on his second set of tyres, was able to pit and come out ahead of Piastri.

"Oh mate, just don't **** talk to me now," he said when told that the Sainz collision had cost them the virtual race lead.

"Nice of you guys to factor that one in by the way, thanks," he added, in reference to the traffic he had to go through.

Already fuming, Piastri was then dealt an even more bitter blow, his gearbox failing on lap 56 forcing him to retire.

After the race though, Piastri said he was simply frustrated by the sequence of events.

"Obviously being taken out by a back marker is never really one of the things you think that can go wrong, but I was proven wrong," Piastri told media after the race.

"I was hoping they wouldn't pit Lando in that moment, to at least give me the chance to stay in the lead," he added.

"But I think that's not very reasonable, so I was more just very upset in the moment about what had happened.

"The timing of my pit stop was fine, we wanted to beat Lewis [Hamilton] and that's what we needed to do."

Lando Norris overtook Oscar Piastri in the opening lap. (Getty Images: Alastair Staley/LAT Images)

McLaren team principle Andrea Stella said he thought both drivers excelled during the race.

"I think today it was actually great racing," he told Sky Sports.

"It was great to see Lando and Oscar fighting at the start for good position, something that was fair.

"Oscar had his own chance to take the lead and see what pace he might have had.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"And how the race unfolded meant that with Oscar we then covered Hamilton and then there was some situation with the backmarkers.

"Lando was very quick once he had the lead and he take advantage of this pace and the fact that there was some delay for Oscar.

"That's racing. We are McLaren racing. It was great racing."

It was also a tough weekend for Ferrari and Lewis Hamilton, who was penalised five seconds for speeding in the pit lane, relegating him to fifth, with his teammate Charles Leclerc in fourth.

Meanwhile, Malaysia's Sepang circuit will host a Formula 1 race for the first time since 2017 as replacement host of the Bahrain Grand Prix.

Liberty Media said in a statement the race will take place on October 4, and would officially be called the 'Gulf Air Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia'.

Follow all the action in our live blog.

World.title: Israeli air strike kills top Hamas official
World.content:
An Israeli air strike has killed a senior officer of the Hamas-run Palestinian internal security service in the Gaza Strip along with his associate.

Colonel Wael El-Ledawi, head of the service in central Gaza, and Major Ramez Abu Zraiq were both killed in the attack as they travelled in a vehicle through Deir Al-Balah in central Gaza.

Israeli military confirmed it had carried out a strike against a Hamas militant, but had not confirmed any further details.

Palestinians inspect the damage to a house targeted by an Israeli strike in Deir al-Balah, in central Gaza Strip. (AP: Abdel Kareem Hana)

The two deaths were confirmed by medics and police officials.

Dozens of members of the Hamas-led police force have been killed by Israeli forces in the past few months, including senior officials.

Israel has accused many of the force of being members of the Hamas armed wing who posed threats to Israel and its forces inside Gaza.

UN alleges Hamas stormed Gaza food depot The UN says the event occurred in the north of the war-ravaged strip, with a senior official saying staff were "endangered."

Hamas says the Israeli attacks on the police force violate the US-brokered October ceasefire between Israel and Hamas.

The ceasefire halted full-scale fighting but has not ended the Israeli strikes from occurring near-daily, Hamas says.

Death toll rises

The deaths of Mr El-Ledawi and Mr Abu Zraiq add to the rising toll of more than 1,190 Palestinians who have been killed by Israeli forces since the ceasefire took effect.

Of those deaths, most were civilians, Gaza health officials report.

Hamas does not usually disclose its losses.

Throughout the same period, four Israeli soldiers have been killed by militants in Gaza.

Six dead after violent clashes in West Bank Violent clashes in the occupied West Bank have left two Israeli soldiers and four Palestinian villagers dead.

Since the 2023 Hamas attack on southern Israel, Israeli forces have effectively taken control of an estimated 64 per cent of the Gaza Strip.

Nearly all of Gaza's population now lives in makeshift tents or damaged buildings in dire conditions under Hamas control.

Reuters

World.title: Victorian premier facing leadership challenge this week
World.content:
Premier Jacinta Allan faces a leadership challenge this week, four months out from the November state election, despite core supporters talking down the threat of a spill.

Factional convenors from both the right and left of the party room met on Sunday night to discuss whether Ms Allan still had the support of a majority of caucus.

The ABC understands they agreed she did not.

A delegation is mooted to approach Ms Allan to allow her to resign on Monday. If she refuses, her leadership is expected to be challenged at Tuesday's caucus meeting when parliament resumes from the winter break.

Cabinet is due to meet on Monday, with plans to set up a new organised crime commission understood to be top of the agenda.

But some loyal MPs are still backing Ms Allan, with senior figures proactively telling the ABC on Sunday night the premier was not going anywhere and that the plan to force her to resign would fail.

But those pushing for change said the premier should resign or face being blown out of office.

"At least [former British PM Sir Keir] Starmer knew when to resign,'' one senior figure said.

They also questioned the blind loyalty to Ms Allan, whose polling numbers have been dire.

"It's not a family, it's a team. We have to act for the good of the government and party,'' the MP said.

Ms Allan has endured months of speculation about her leadership over worsening poll results and her response to alleged corruption in the taxpayer-funded Big Build.

A growing cohort of Labor MPs believe the government needs to launch a royal commission into the scandal, which Ms Allan has ruled out. There is a view among Labor sources that changing leaders would also require a shift in focus.

Labor sources have been despairing about the possibility of a wipe-out at the November 28 election, and many had formed the view that Ms Allan was unable to recover in the polls.

Members from around the country gathered in Adelaide for the party's national conference, where senior figures debated Ms Allan's position.

'Bad with him, but diabolical with her'

Deputy Premier Ben Carroll is the most likely candidate to usurp Ms Allan.

He has previously ruled out challenging. But if Ms Allan concedes she has lost the support of caucus, this would pave the way for Mr Carroll to become leader through a vacancy.

Deputy Premier Ben Carroll has previously ruled out challenging Ms Allan. (ABC News)

One MP, speaking anonymously, said the view was that the party's position would be "bad with him, but diabolical with her".

However, Ms Allan's internal supporters were continuing to hose down the speculation on Sunday night.

Planning Minister Sonya Kilkenny earlier dismissed the chatter as "idle gossip".

"She has my full support," Kilkenny told reporters on Sunday morning.

Not all MPs had received a call to test their support for a coup by Sunday night.

If caucus forged ahead with a successful spill and Ms Allan still contested a leadership ballot, the entire Victorian Labor membership would get a vote in a weeks-long process.

"It would be chaos,'' one MP said.

MPs opposed to any change say not all caucus members, or sub-factions, have been consulted.

One senior was adamant, saying "the premier is not going away. She has the numbers."

Others have speculated that the push, and the briefing out to media of the plans, is designed to build momentum, rather than a full majority declaring they want a change of leadership.

Ms Allan became premier in September 2023 following the resignation of Daniel Andrews.

Her Bendigo East seat is under threat from the Nationals.

World.title: Teens charged after alleged machete brawl in Melbourne's CBD
World.content:
Police have charged four young people, who were all on bail, after an alleged machete brawl in Melbourne's CBD early on Sunday morning.

Two people received serious injuries during the altercation at the intersection of Elizabeth and Flinders streets, near Flinders Station.

Police said the incident occurred at about 5am after a verbal dispute between two females escalated.

"Others within their respective groups got involved," a spokesperson said.

"The incident escalated and one male brandishing a machete chased two males and allegedly slashed both, causing serious injuries to the hand of one male and the arm of the other."

Six people, aged between 16 and 23, were arrested in relation to the incident.

Four of those were charged with various offences, including committing an indictable offence while on bail.

A 17-year-old male from the Brimbank area was also charged with intentionally causing injury in circumstances of gross violence, affray, as well as possessing a prohibited weapon and drugs.

A 19-year-old man from Bacchus Marsh and a 16-year-old female from the Banyule area were both charged with affray, while a 23-year-old man from Laverton was charged with theft.

The 16- and 23-year-olds were let out on bail to appear in court at a later date.

Police said they gave a 17-year-old girl a caution for possession of drugs, while another young woman was released without charge.

The investigation continues, and police have urged any witnesses to come forward with information.

World.title: WA government considering new gas-fired power plant as coal phases out
World.content:
The Western Australian government is investigating building and running a new gas-fired power plant in the south of Perth as it prepares to switch off coal by 2030.

The government has identified a site at Naval Base for a 300-megawatt (MW) power station that is expected to cost more than half a billion dollars.

WA Premier Roger Cook said his government was committed to being the "first and only state" to switch off "all our state-owned coal-fired power stations by 2030".

"A clean energy transition involves renewable energy, backed by battery and firmed by gas," he told reporters on Sunday.

"That's why we need to do careful planning; I stress at this stage we are just going to the community consultation and planning phase."

The state will not be increasing its reliance on gas, according to the WA government.

Roger Cook says his government is committed to shutting all state-owned coal-fired power stations by 2030.

Mr Cook said this project, like the gas turbines at the Pinjar power station that was commissioned in 1989, would "replace existing assets that are coming to the end of their lives".

The energy needed to replace coal would come from renewables, including wind farms in the Mid-West, a government spokesperson said.

However, the state government has not put a price tag on the proposed project as it is still at an early stage.

Mr Cook says the proposed project aims to replace aging assets that are due to retire. (Supplied: APR)

This year, independent operator AGL stated it funded a similar 220-megawatt expansion at its Kwinana Swift Power Station for $450 million.

The ABC understands the state-owned project will be bigger and without existing infrastructure, with the cost expected to be higher.

A decision on the gas project is expected by the end of the year, as the state government is under pressure to meet its 2030 goals.

Bipartisan support

The project has rare bipartisan support, with the opposition suggesting it had the idea first.

"I do support this plan, because we built the exact same plan … two years ago," said WA Liberal energy spokesman Steve Thomas.

But Mr Thomas said the proposed power plant needed to do more than just replace existing gas turbines, if coal was to be switched off.

Steve Thomas says the state government needs new and additional gas to meet its goal. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

"There is no way the government is closing down its coal fleet, on its current time frame, unless they have significantly more gas generation; that means they need new and additional gas, not just replacing old units," he told the ABC.

"They will need to have more than 300MW of new gas in total if they are going to keep the lights on past 2029."

He added that it would be "another failure of the transition plan" if the government was not putting more gas generation into the system.

"Some of the Pinjar units are due to retire in the mid-2030's, which means that this replacement is not really needed until then, which means in the meantime it is additional gas generation capacity."

The project will open to public consultation this week.

World.title: Hopes US and Iran will return to negotiating table after lull in hostilities
World.content:
Iran has passed another night without US air strikes, as Washington pauses a war nearing its fifth month and reports emerge that concerns over dwindling munitions were restraining plans for further escalation.

The lull has revived hopes of a return to negotiations after nearly two weeks of consecutive nightly US bombardments, although US media reported the pause could also reflect pressure on stockpiles of Patriot interceptors and other defensive weapons.

Houthis claim missile attacks on Saudi Arabia The Iran-backed Houthi rebels have claimed a missile attack on Saudia Arabia's cities of Jazan and Yanbu.

Iran would halt attacks as long as the United States maintained its pause on strikes, a senior Iranian source said, adding that Tehran remained sceptical of US intentions.

"Iran's position remains 'attack for ‌attack': if the ‌attacks stop, Iran will also halt its operations. That message has already been conveyed to the United States," the source ⁠told Reuters a ‌day after Washington ‌halted attacks following 13 successive nights ‌of air strikes.

"There is more ‌scepticism than ⁠optimism about the halt in attacks. The prevailing view is that the pause ⁠is tactical rather than genuine," the source ‌said.

It comes as US ambassador to the United Nations ‌Mike Waltz said President Donald Trump had paused attacks to allow more room for diplomacy.

"He's giving talks some space, he's giving it a little bit of room," Mr Waltz told Fox News on Sunday.

Meanwhile, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said he would be visiting Washington on Monday, on Mr Trump's invitation.

"I will also discuss all pending issues with President Trump, including the situation in Iran," he said on X.

Fighting over the strategic Strait of Hormuz derailed diplomatic efforts between Washington and Tehran, but the conflict then expanded beyond the vital energy corridor to include attacks on US bases, regional shipping and Gulf allies.

However, US operations against Iran were "on a hold", CNN reported, quoting an unidentified Pentagon source, even as Mr Trump threatened a "much higher level" of strikes on Friday.

Plans to escalate the campaign have been shelved in part because of those shrinking supplies, The New York Times reported, citing two people briefed on the matter.

Mr Trump also faces the risk of a wider Middle East war, the estrangement of vulnerable Gulf allies and further shocks to the global economy, the newspaper said.

US Vice-President JD Vance and top general Dan Caine both raised concerns about escalation at a White House meeting on Friday, CNN reported.

General Caine told Mr Trump the military could carry out the options available to him successfully but warned of the possible implications, according to the network.

Trump undecided

Mr Trump said on Friday he had not decided whether to return to an all-out operation.

"We're talking to them right now. I think they're getting more and more serious," he said.

Mr Trump said Iran faced a choice between a deal and strikes at a "much higher level".

Donald Trump says he has not decided whether to return to an all-out operation against Iran. (AP: Rod Lamkey, Jr)

The war that Mr Trump once predicted would last four or five weeks is now nearing its fifth month, and is weighing on the Republicans' approval ratings ahead of crucial US midterm elections in November.

The Pentagon had presented Mr Trump with a plan for a 14th night of strikes but he declined to authorise it in favour of a push for talks, Axios reported.

Fighting spreads

Fighting has spread to a new front.

Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels said they struck Saudi Aramco sites in Jizan and Yanbu on Saturday, a day after Riyadh bombed Houthi targets.

A surface-to-air battery operated by Greek personnel in Saudi Arabia downed two ballistic missiles and a drone over Yanbu, the Greek air force media office said.

US and Iran trade strikes The strikes came after US President Donald Trump vowed "major military punishment" for Tehran and its Houthi allies in Yemen over moves to block a second major international shipping route.

Iran's Revolutionary Guards said they had stopped four ships attempting to transit the Strait of Hormuz in 24 hours.

Tehran's effective blockade of the waterway remains the central flashpoint with Washington.

Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Iran could not be blamed for the escalation and offered to broker talks between the Houthis and Riyadh, saying "there is no military solution".

ABC/AFP/Reuters

World.title: ‘You idiot’: Piastri’s big blow-up as Hungarian Grand Prix unravels
World.content:
SportMotorsportFormula 1 ‘You idiot’: Piastri’s big blow-up as Hungarian Grand Prix unravels Hannah Kennelly July 27, 2026 — 2:45am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Oscar Piastri managed to have one of the best and worst races of his career on Sunday. His start was stupendous – getting past Ferrari’s Charles Leclerc and overtaking pole-sitter and teammate Lando Norris on the opening lap to lead the Hungarian Grand Pix. After a rough start to his 2026 campaign, it looked like this was finally Piastri’s moment, a legitimate chance for a grand prix win or a podium. Oscar Piastri has notched another DNF for his 2026 season. Clive Rose Piastri managed to hold Norris at bay for nearly half the race. Then it all went pear-shaped.



McLaren decided to pit Piastri on lap 34 and chose to keep Norris out to avoid Lewis Hamilton undercutting the McLarens. Piastri came into the pits, but was later caught behind back markers (slower cars that are about to be lapped) including Carlos Sainz, who clipped his front wheel. “Get out of the f---ing way, you idiot! Oh my God,” Piastri said over the radio. View post on X Moments later, Norris – who stayed longer on his second set of tyres – was able to pit and emerged in front of Piastri. The Australian’s race engineer informed Piastri over team radio that the collision with Sainz had cost him the lead of the race.



“Oh mate, just don’t **** talk to me now,” Piastri said in an uncharacteristic display of frustration. Piastri proceeded to criticise McLaren’s strategy, pointing out they put him in a situation where he would encounter traffic. “Nice of you guys to factor that one in by the way, thanks,” he said. View post on X On lap 56, Piastri’s McLaren spluttered to a halt on the side of the track, with a suspected gearbox failure. With 14 laps to go, his race was over and the Australian added another DNF to his resume.





The Australian star also had to deal with increasing rumours around the safety of his seat amid reports Verstappen is seeking an end to his Red Bull tenure. McLaren team principal Andrea Stella said it was good to see Norris and Piastri “fighting at the start for good position”, hailing it as “great racing”. Lando Norris won the Hungarian Grand Prix. Getty Images “Oscar had his own chance to take the lead and see what pace he might have had,” he told Sky Sports. “How the race unfolded meant that with Oscar we then covered Hamilton and then there was some situation with the backmarkers. Lando was very quick once he had the lead and he took advantage of the pace and the fact that there was some delay for Oscar.



“That’s racing. We are McLaren racing. It was great racing.” Speaking to media post-race, Piastri appeared more composed, and was his usual straightforward self. “I’m feeling pretty disappointed,” he said. “I feel like lap one was good, the first stint in general was reasonable and then struggled for pace on the hard ... but I had track position, and I felt like even though I was struggling, it felt like I could hang on, but from that point on, pretty much everything that could have gone wrong did. “On the strategy side, you don’t plan a strategy for getting taken out by a backmarker. So I can’t blame the team at all for that.

World.title: Wildfires threaten Bordeaux as France, Spain battle blazes
World.content:
WorldEuropeExtreme weather Wildfires threaten Bordeaux as France, Spain battle blazes Manuel Ausloos and David Latona July 27, 2026 — 2:34am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Bordeaux/Madrid: Wildfires advanced toward the outskirts of the historic French city of Bordeaux at the heart of the country’s winelands on Sunday as France and Spain battled blazes that have already forced the evacuation of hundreds of thousands of people. About 220,000 people have been evacuated in France, while in Spain more than 75,000 people have had to leave their homes and around 30,000 more were ordered to shelter in place, authorities said. A firefighter battles a wildfire in San Martin de Valdeiglesias, west of Madrid, Spain, on Sunday. AP Photo/Manu Fernandez In France, fires have ravaged the Cap Ferret peninsula on the Atlantic coast, a popular tourist destination, and spread through areas surrounding Bordeaux, where firefighters were trying to prevent the flames from reaching the regional capital. “The fire is about 15 kilometres away from the entry points to the main city,” Bordeaux Mayor Thomas Cazenave said on Sunday, while Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said on X that the situation remained “difficult”.



Footage released by French police showed officers knocking on doors at night in the municipalities of Marcheprime and Cestas to evacuate homes one by one. Related Article Heatwave Europe’s summers are changing. The continent isn’t ready In Spain, Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez visited fire-hit areas in Avila, one of three central provinces affected by major blazes alongside Madrid and Toledo, where more than 45,000 hectares (111,000 acres) have burned. Spain battles multiple blazes A separate blaze in Spain’s eastern Castellon province has ravaged more than 4300 hectares, regional authorities said.



“The fire is out of control, it’s very difficult to extinguish from a technical standpoint, especially because of the adverse weather conditions that will continue throughout the day,” the regional leader of Valencia, Juanfran Perez, told reporters near the site. The wildfire has entered the Sierra de Espadan natural park, which contains large forests of pine trees and cork oaks. The fires are the latest disasters linked to prolonged drought and successive heatwaves that scientists say have been intensified by climate change. In both Bordeaux and Avila, July high temperatures have averaged 32 degrees Celsius, almost 6 degrees above the month’s normal high between 1961 and 1990, according to the Reuters Climate Monitor. International aid mobilised



Under the European Union’s civil protection mechanism, Greece and Italy have each sent two Canadair firefighting aircraft to Spain, while Portugal has deployed more than 100 military personnel along with equipment. Two more planes will arrive “as soon as possible” from Turkey, the Spanish interior ministry said on X. Loading Sanchez said his government would on Tuesday declare a civil protection emergency for the central provinces plagued by the wildfires, unlocking additional recovery funding. More than 150,000 hectares have burned across Spain since January, he said, six times the area destroyed during the same period last year.



While wildfires have long been a feature of Spain’s summers, Sanchez said their growing scale and intensity, fuelled by increasingly extreme weather, required policies grounded in climate science. More fires in Scotland, Italy In the highlands of Scotland, as many as 500 firefighters have been dealing with a large blaze within Cairngorms National Park since July 15. Residents of the village of Nethy Bridge, who were evacuated on Friday evening after a change in weather conditions, were allowed to return to their homes late on Saturday. A firefighter takes a break while battling a wildfire near Le Temple, outside Bordeaux. AP Photo/Emma Da Silva



A burnt vehicle sits outside a charred house in Navas del Rey, west of Madrid. AP Photo/Manu Fernandez In Italy, several bushfires forced the closure of a southern section of the Rome ring road as well as a motorway leading into the capital, causing major traffic disruption. In Italy’s southern Puglia region, tourists were evacuated from seaside resorts due to a large wildfire in the Gargano area, the national fire department said. Some were taken away by sea by the coast guard, the ANSA news agency added. Pope Leo, speaking from his summer residence of Castel Gandolfo outside Rome, offered spiritual support. “In light of the devastating wildfires that have affected various areas of France and Spain in recent days, I wish to express my solidarity and closeness, and I invite everyone to pray for those affected and for the rescue workers engaged in relief efforts,” he said.

World.title: ‘I’m sorry ... but’: Apologetic Alan Joyce tells his side of the Qantas story
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesAviation ‘I’m sorry ... but’: Apologetic Alan Joyce tells his side of the Qantas story Chris Zappone July 27, 2026 — 12:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Worse than the global financial crisis. Worse than the aftermath of the September 11 attacks. A shock to the industry that could cost the company 10,000 jobs. In 2020, these predictions of the damage COVID-19 would wreak on the aviation industry were ringing in the ears of the Qantas board and chief executive Alan Joyce when the “Flying Kangaroo” announced it would sack 1820 ground crew. The High Court later ruled the workers were sacked illegally and many are still waiting for compensation. Former Qantas chief executive Alan Joyce: “I apologise for the angst that was generated.” Louie Douvis It is only now, six years later – and three after stepping down as Qantas’ CEO – that Joyce has expressed some regret. His admission comes with caveats. Joyce says that if in August 2020, someone had told him “... on the other end of this there was going to be a vaccine, the vaccine was going to be effective, and that when the vaccine was going to work, there would be a massive rebound in demand – absolutely you would have made different decisions”.



“So with the information we had at the time, I still don’t think there was any other decision you could make,” he told this masthead during a video call from his Sydney home. “Hindsight is a great thing.” Speaking ahead of the launch of his book, Alan Joyce: Riding the Jet Stream, this week, Joyce said that despite his regrets, he cannot explain the post-lockdown resentment that continues to linger among the public. ‘I was the frog in the proverbial hot water and I didn’t know how hot it had gotten.’ Alan Joyce That’s perhaps not surprising from a man who, during his near 15-year tenure in the cockpit of Australia’s national airline, was not well known for his contrition. In moments of organisational chaos, political controversy and the “ghost flights” scandal, he was not prone to apology. Even now, the bottom line in Joyce’s mind was the bottom line of the company: Qantas survived COVID intact, and its shareholders didn’t lose a cent.



For Joyce, who spent an earlier portion of his career at Ansett Australia, keeping an airline alive is not academic. He had a front-row seat to Ansett’s collapse, having been its head of network planning when he left the company in 2000. It collapsed in 2001. Editor's pick Aviation Alan Joyce has been writing his book. Here’s how five people illegally sacked by his airline have fared “I’m actually very, very proud of the fact that I’m not sitting here and apologising for Qantas going bankrupt, [something] that many airlines around the world did,” Joyce says, pointing to the dozens of airlines around the world that went bankrupt, forced into mergers or put under administration during that period of time. That tally included Virgin Australia in 2020. “I think we would have caused more problems, more angst, if I was sitting here, and apologising for Qantas going bankrupt.” Qantas posted losses in 2021 and 2022 as COVID brought the business to a standstill, with an underlying loss before tax of $1.8 billion, only to swing decisively to a $2.4 billion profit in 2023 as public fury mounted over spiralling ticket prices and abysmal service outcomes. Joyce resigned two months early in September 2023.



Credit where it’s due Public anger compounded after the so-called “ghost flight” scandal, in which the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission fined Qantas $120 million for selling tickets for 8000 already cancelled flights. During COVID, Qantas appeared to bank up to $1.6 billion COVID travel credits that customers were unable to use amid mass flight cancellations triggered by border closures. The company did not clearly inform customers they were entitled to refunds. Under pressure, Qantas repeatedly extended the refund deadlines. It also agreed to a $105 million settlement following a class action against Qantas over the COVID-19 flight credits. Competitor Virgin, Joyce notes, just pocketed nearly $93 million because their credits expired. A Virgin spokesperson said: “More than 90 per cent of COVID credits were redeemed by guests”. Qantas has since removed all expiry dates and the outstanding amount remains on the balance sheet. The credits Qantas holds were worth $240 million as of December 31, 2025.



“I apologise for the angst that was generated [for] the customers on it, but the reality was we had 22 million bookings in the system [and] the system wasn’t designed to do an automatic refund,” he said. On many of Joyce or the airline’s most notable public controversies, his responses follow this familiar formula: “I’m sorry, but … “We were trying to fix things on the go, but it got a lot better as we went through it... Eventually, we got there and probably had the best policy of any airline out there,” he says. ‘Part of the job’ Few in corporate Australia have faced scrutiny or public pressure in the way Joyce did, particularly through the latter stages of his tenure. At Qantas, he says, they joked about the “Himalayas of brand reporting,” referring to the drastic peaks and troughs of consumer sentiment.



Joyce faced white-hot anger from airline customers during his time at the helm. In 2024, a best-selling book by journalist Joe Aston probing the company’s dealings with politicians captured public attention. Some singled him out over the airline’s stance on social issues. Joyce, now happily married to his long-term partner Shane Lloyd, was criticised for the organisation’s support of the “Yes” campaign for marriage equality in 2017. Two-thirds of Australians voted supporting the campaign, but that didn’t stop a protester smashing a pie into Joyce’s face while he spoke on stage at a Perth event. When senior Coalition politician Peter Dutton criticised a group of CEOs who signed a letter supporting the campaign, Joyce was the one he singled out. Joyce endured attacks and criticism over the company’s position on social issues. That aside, Joyce doesn’t see himself as a victim, or a fall guy for post-lockdown resentment. He accepts “because it was part of the job”, the bouts of extreme criticism he was at times subjected to. He also laments what he describes as the reluctance of corporate leaders to advocate on political and social issues as Qantas did in 2017 and in 2023, when the company supported the unsuccessful referendum campaign for an Indigenous Voice to parliament.



“I think there’s obviously fewer people doing it, if any, and I think that’s a shame because I think corporations are part of society,” he says. Editor's pick Updated

Aviation Qantas to pay $105m after class action over cancelled COVID flights On whether broader societal discontent in the post-COVID years played a role in the criticism, he said: “I really can’t answer that because I certainly don’t have any post-lockdown resentment.” “Maybe some people in the community do, but I certainly don’t.” Of Aston’s book, The Chairman’s Lounge, Joyce denied its claim he upgraded Prime Minister Anthony Albanese’s son to the lounge, an invitation-only club usually reserved for politicians and business leaders.



The book also alleged Joyce arranged flight upgrades for the prime minister and senior politicians. He said others in the company had the ability to arrange upgrades. “I do not remember him ever ringing me asking for an upgrade. I had to get my PA to do it on a computer … I rang her when the claim came out,” he says. “She said she had no memory of ever doing it for me. Anytime I did an upgrade I signed a document. I believe the documentation was checked and there’s no document for me signing.” Prime Minister Anthony Albanese with former Qantas chief executive Alan Joyce in 2023. AAP The exit lounge Ultimately, Joyce’s legacy echoes at higher volume within the aviation industry than it does in the public arena or political circles.



When Joyce stepped down as CEO, trust in the Qantas brand was at a low ebb and his replacement, Vanessa Hudson, who was chief financial officer under Joyce, is seeking to rebuild it. Other parts of his handover were brighter. Budget subsidiary Jetstar, of which Joyce was the founding CEO, remains profitable and has announced a slew of new routes despite rising fuel costs. Project Sunrise, a Joyce brainchild to connect Sydney to London non-stop appears to be on track for the first flights to begin next year, with the specially adapted Airbus A350 having visited Melbourne last week. Internationally, Joyce remains a respected voice in global aviation, having served as chairman of the oneworld governing board, as well as chairman of the board of governors for the International Air Transport Association. It wasn’t until his first year after leaving, while decompressing from 15 years as CEO, that he realised the full extent of the high-pressure situation he was in during his twilight months in the role. “I was the frog in the proverbial hot water and I didn’t know how hot it had gotten,” he says.



He spent that year enjoying a quieter life with husband Shane and travelled back to Ireland to look after his mother. Joyce was later persuaded to write the book, which he described as a “cathartic experience”. Loading Uncertain future Asked about the impact of the unfolding Middle East conflict on global aviation, Joyce said the situation could go either way and executives would be preparing for a wide range of scenarios – everything from another ceasefire and a return to normal (in which case oil prices drop and demand surges). Or the conflict could widen to the point that not just the Persian Gulf is closed, but also the Red Sea. If so, that’s when “you get into really bad territory for airlines”.



Joyce, who studied physics and mathematics at the Dublin Institute of Technology and later studied at Trinity College, said airlines would be examining the probability of each scenario. If the conflict paralyses oil shipments, “it doesn’t matter how much you’re willing to pay, you just don’t get supply”. That situation would be something akin to “COVID without the masks”, Joyce said, and flights would be grounded again. After reading Joyce’s book and listening to him discuss his career at length, one can have no doubt that if he was still in charge of an airline navigating the challenges coming out of the Middle East, there would be no question about his approach. He would listen to the experts and take whatever action he thought necessary to protect the company, however drastic, no matter the personal cost. And he wouldn’t apologise for it. World.title: Extraordinary meeting of Labor conveners resolves to move against Jacinta Allan
World.content:
An internal Labor Party campaign to dump Jacinta Allan as Victorian premier reached a critical stage on Sunday night after an extraordinary meeting of factional conveners resolved to move against her leadership. The meeting of conveners from across the party’s Left and Right factions was called to determine whether Allan has the caucus backing she needs to lead the government to the state election on November 28. Four sources with knowledge of the meeting said the room broadly agreed that after nearly three years as Premier, Allan’s days in the top job are numbered. It is less clear how a leadership challenge will unfold. A meeting of factional conveners on Sunday night resolved to dump Jacinta Allan as the leader of Victorian Labor. Michael Howard One source told The Age that the premier had been informed on Sunday night that she had lost the support of the Labor caucus.



A defiant Allan, who spent Sunday night at her home in Bendigo with senior advisers, told her supporters that, regardless of what the factional chiefs decide, she would not resign. The leadership manoeuvres are taking place in the absence of a declared challenger. Allan’s most likely replacement, Deputy Premier Ben Carroll, has indicated to colleagues that while he would be a contender if the leadership became vacant, he would not use his numbers to bring the premier down. Deputy Premier Ben Carroll has been touted as Allan’s most likely replacement. Alex Coppel A contested leadership ballot, just four months out from a state election, would paralyse the government.



Under previously untested party rules, a new leader would be chosen by a caucus vote and ballot of party members, with even weight given to both. The process can take up to six weeks. In the event of a leadership spill, the deputy leader steps in to run the government. If Allan and Carroll are leadership candidates, both would be sidelined from their day jobs and an interim leader appointed. There is consternation among some MPs, particularly in the dominant Left faction, that the factional conveners did not sufficiently canvass the views of parliamentarians within their respective groups before Sunday night’s meeting. The Age has spoken to seven Victorian Labor sources who say they believe Allan would lose if her leadership came to a vote of the party’s 69 MPs. But one MP told The Age not every faction was represented at the Sunday night meeting and downplayed its significance.



“The premier absolutely has the numbers,” they said. “Some people don’t want to do the hard work. They want things on a plate and I can tell you now the caucus are there behind the premier.” As with the last round of leadership rumblings in June, the pathway for a coup is littered with assumptions that have not yet been realised. Multiple sources from both factions agreed it would be difficult for Carroll, who sits on the Right, to challenge Allan – despite some within her own Left faction wanting him to do so – after he publicly ruled out a challenge at a press conference last month. After looking the premier in the eye and declaring he would not challenge her for the leadership, Carroll told reporters, “I’ve got a young daughter at home, and I couldn’t be more proud to make sure that she grows up knowing that I supported Jacinta Allan to be a world-class premier and get re-elected in her own right.”



Another option being considered is a delegation of factional leaders speaking to Allan and asking her to step aside. Two sources said they found it difficult to believe Allan would go down without a fight, but conceded it was not impossible that she could be convinced if it were clear she no longer had the numbers in caucus. A supporter of Allan, speaking on the condition of anonymity to talk freely, said if the Sunday night meeting showed a majority of MPs wanted a change of leadership, the premier could face a vote of no confidence at Tuesday’s caucus meeting. “It would be a very brave premier that continued in light of an unfavourable outcome,” they said.



Attorney-General Sonya Kilkenny, speaking earlier on Sunday, said the leadership speculation was “idle gossip”. Related Article Exclusive

Victorian election Revealed: Secret government plan to tackle organised crime “She has my full support, and this idle gossip doesn’t help Victorians,” she said. “It is only hurting Victorians at a time when Victorians need us all to be focused on them, and that is exactly what Jacinta Allan and our Labor government, our team, is doing.” Over the past week, a range of new policies have leaked from the Premier’s Private Office that suggest Allan’s team is trying to find announcements that could mollify her colleagues. On Monday, cabinet will consider a proposal to create a new agency within Victoria Police that targets organised crime and is informed by Australia’s best criminal intelligence.



The policy has been viewed internally as a way to kill off pressure for a royal commission into Big Build corruption, tying the issue together with other political problems such as an increase in firebombings in Melbourne, and community concerns about youth crime rates. Another leaked policy floated amending the rate cap rules to allow councils to better recoup the costs needed to pay staff – a policy supported by the Australian Services Union but quickly seized on by the opposition as a cost-of-living attack. One MP said Allan was in denial about her support and rather than step aside would likely enforce party rules for a spill, which requires a vote of the Labor membership if the caucus result is contested. But they also said those conspiring needed to “piss or get off the pot”. A senior Labor figure said Allan’s leadership had been doomed, and she was now incredibly unpopular despite being given time to connect with voters.



Related Article Analysis

Building Bad Nobody measures ‘Bandidos kickbacks’: How construction costs took CFMEU centre stage “There is now an opportunity to push the reset button, give confidence back to voters and remind voters of the benefits of a strong Labor government.” The latest Resolve Political Monitor has Allan’s likeability at minus 36, her equal lowest result on record. Opposition Leader Jess Wilson maintains a lead on preferred premier, with 43 per cent of voters saying they want her to lead the state compared with 24 per cent for Allan. More Victorian politics:

World.title: Markel ado about nothing? The verdict on Meghan as guest MasterChef judge
World.content:
FoodMasterChef Recap Markel ado about nothing? The verdict on Meghan as guest MasterChef judge The Duchess of Sussex makes her much-hyped appearance on MasterChef and shares her not-so-famous home cooking expertise with the giddy amateur cooks. Ben Pobjie July 26, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

And so it came to pass, that Meghan Duchess of Sussex arrived at the MasterChef kitchen, and just like Poochie the Dog, she made life worthwhile for us all. And what a spectacular entrance it was. After Poh gives her a grand and really quite misleading introduction – describing her as a “global icon” and someone known for her “home cooking”, so that nobody could possibly guess who it might be – the woman herself walks down the red carpet to widespread bafflement. Meghan and her impressive table of produce under the chandeliers. Channel Ten/Kelly Gardner As well as the final four amateur cooks, all eliminated contestants were allowed to be in the room to witness the royal event, and every one of them performs impressive impressions of people who are impressed. The sense that Meghan’s presence in the kitchen is utterly inexplicable, however, is impossible to miss – if Robert Irwin as a guest judge was confusing, this is bewilderment on a scale rarely seen on Australian television since the demise of It’s A Knockout. Many people might have questioned the Duchess’s credentials as a cooking expert, but those people are immediately shut up when she revealed a table full of fruits and vegetables and demonstrates that she knows all their names and how to pronounce them properly (as opposed to the word “herb”, which she pronounces wrongly because she is American).



Meghan, Duchess of Sussex on the set of MasterChef Australia Channel 10/Supplied Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up “Your time starts now,” she announces, showing all the acting chops she honed on Suits, as she plays the part of a person who has the slightest interest in anyone else in the room. As the cooks rush to make their dishes – the task was to take an ingredient and make a meal “fit for a duchess”, or more specifically fit for a duchess who has been excluded from the royal family – the judges surround Meghan to tell her how wonderful she is and ask her what she would cook and how she got to be so beautiful and what brand of shampoo she uses. The cooks themselves come up with all kinds of crazy concepts, but we wouldn’t want to dwell on those. As the old TV industry aphorism goes, if you want people to pay attention to the food, you do not get Meghan on as a guest judge. It is notable, however, that Aaron appears to have a crush on Meghan and is quite flustered when talking to her about carrots. Incidentally, carrots are one of the many vegetables that Meghan ABSOLUTELY LOVES. Petro makes celeriac ice-cream, in line with his well-earned reputation as “guy who makes desserts out of ludicrous things”. And it was a wise choice for the guest judge too, because Meghan LOVES celeriac. And she LOVES the idea of celeriac ice-cream. And she LOVES being on television. Neither Petro nor Aaron can believe they are cooking for Meghan, who, to be clear, is not just an ordinary human being: she is an ordinary human being who married someone very famous. As such she makes all those other guest judges who have achieved massive success in food by their talent and years of hard work really look like pathetic losers.



Meghan LOVES celeriac. And she LOVES the idea of celeriac ice-cream. And she LOVES being on television. At one point, Poh drags Meghan over to a table and makes her eat her banana and date loaf, just so they can say the duchess really earned her fee. Meghan asks Poh if she can have the recipe and Poh says she can, both knowing that in an hour or so they will part ways and never talk to each other again for the rest of their lives. There is also some cooking going on – Vinnie, like Petro, is using celeriac, but unlike Petro is being normal and not making ice-cream out of it. Instead he is cooking a steak and draping celeriac in decorative ways over it. Meghan is SO EXCITED about this. Meanwhile, Casper has an artichoke. “That artichoke looks wild!” shout the watchers from the balcony, where they’re really starved of things to get excited about now they’ve all talked about how INSANE and CRAZY and UNBELIEVABLE it is to have Meghan here. Quickly we cut away from the cooking to listen to Meghan talk about her show, With Love, Meghan, which is just like MasterChef apparently because it’s all about “cooking for joy”. Also, just like MasterChef contestants, Meghan has no qualifications or experience as a professional cook, so there are a lot of parallels.



But you can’t deny that she’s got a real knack for walking up to people and telling them there’s 30 minutes left. So good at this is she, in fact, that after she tells all four contestants, everyone gives her a round of applause. And why not? They just watched a woman walk around a room without falling over and say several words – not everyone can do this! “It feels like she’s looking into your soul,” says Casper, possibly hinting that Meghan might secretly be a demon? This is backed up when he immediately cuts himself for the first time this season. The Duchess’s powers are indeed terrifying, as the blood flows in the kitchen. Casper has a vision for cooking octopus, and Meghan LOVES that. “Make it sparkle for Meghan Markle!” Sofia shouts, and doggone it that is just about the most brilliant bit of wordplay anyone present has ever heard. The kitchen practically explodes with happiness. Shortly after this, Petro says a sequence of words that has never been spoken before in human history: “My concern with the ice-cream is that there might not be enough celeriac.” So this episode is historic for two reasons. Meghan then tastes Petro’s ice-cream and immediately assumes an expression of intense distress, as if she’s just been forced to watch a dog being strangled. It is a moment of high panic as Petro contemplates the likelihood that he is about to serve the worst plate of food ever made to an actual duchess/fictional lawyer. But he still has time to try to make it taste non-horrible. It’s celeriac ice-cream so he probably can’t, but he can try.



Judges Jean Christophe Novelli looking cranky, Poh Ling Yeow, Meghan and Sofia Levin. Ten The judging process is incredibly tense: Casper’s octopus, Vinnie’s steak, Petro’s ice-cream and Aaron’s stir-fry must compete not only against each other, but also against the impossibly refined palate of Meghan Markle, Ethereal Super-Being. There’s also tension emanating from Jean-Christophe, who’s looked pissed off for the whole episode, as if he’s itching to ask Meghan how many Michelin stars she’s got. But the Duchess comes through with some truly penetrating insights into the food she eats, like “I love this dish” and “It’s so good”. You can definitely see how she became a Duchess, a title traditionally granted only to the most discerning of reality TV cooking judges. The most amazing part of the judging is when a producer suddenly walks into shot and hands Meghan a phone, on which Prince Harry himself is Facetiming! Isn’t that amazing? Just on the spur of the moment it happened! I’ve never seen anything so spontaneous and unplanned! Everyone again bursts into applause for the concept of unearned privilege. Anyway in the end everyone loves every dish, even Petro’s psychotic ice-cream. In fact, it’s the dish of the day and Petro goes through to the semi-final, proving the ironclad rule of MasterChef: put something stupid in ice-cream and you’ll win. The judges thank Meghan for coming all this way just to earn a large amount of money and promote her brand, and everyone is happy, especially Meghan, who now gets to go to her hotel room and forget about it. As for the rest of us, we can only sit back, spent, and wonder, as a civilisation, what we have wrought. Related Article Opinion So, Meghan’s going on MasterChef? Our resident show expert shares his thoughts Ben Pobjie Entertainment writer

World.title: ‘We stand by our decision to play him’: Lyon feels the heat after King’s AFL comeback ends early
World.content:
Updated SportAFLAFL 2026 ‘We stand by our decision to play him’: Lyon feels the heat after King’s AFL comeback ends early Marc McGowan Updated July 26, 2026 — 9:48pm ,first published 5:29pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

St Kilda coach Ross Lyon is adamant tortured St Kilda spearhead Max King was ready to play on Sunday despite his first AFL game in 757 days ending prematurely due to hamstring tightness. King’s latest setback in a challenging period for the 26-year-old marred the Saints’ 31-point win over fellow wildcard contender North Melbourne at Marvel Stadium, including a four-goal-to-one final quarter that transformed a competitive contest into a comfortable victory. Max King in full flight during Sunday’s match. AFL Photos via Getty Images Resident superstar Nasiah Wanganeen-Milera was the difference again, kicking three of his four goals after going forward in the third quarter as part of a 46-disposal performance that ripped the match away from the Kangaroos. Lyon did not speak to King before his post-game media conference, but said that the star forward would undergo scans on Monday to assess any potential damage. The coach backed his medical staff’s decision to give King the green light after he suffered a hamstring strain in a VFL game in May.



Related Article Investigation

AFL off-field behaviour Crime threats, nude pics and a Tinder date: Inside the AFL’s most secretive unit “I don’t even know what the outcome is, so how can it be an error before there’s an outcome?” Lyon said. “But we stand by our decision to play him. We have high-performance experts, we have [training] load, we have conditioning. We’re really quite confident. “In the four-week [rehabilitation] block, he had 50 per cent more volume of high-speed running, and 500 per cent more very high-speed running, which is above 24 kilometres [an hour]. His biggest sessions were game-load sessions with 20 per cent more. “So, in the context of that evidence, our conditioners thought [he was ready], and game time was only 12 minutes a quarter – two six-minute stints. It was very considered, very worked out, and I’m happy for it to sit with me and our team because we collaborate.”



King had just one kick – a long set shot from the boundary in the second quarter – and one handball in limited game time, but left the ground for good only 13 minutes into the third term. He went to the rooms soon after and did not reappear before the Saints ruled him out. King’s hamstring strain in May added to the knee and calf setbacks which stalled a promising career that was stuck on 83 games for more than two years. Speaking post-match to SEN, St Kilda veteran Brad Hill was hopeful King had avoided another lengthy lay-off. Nasiah Wanganeen-Milera, being embraced by teammate Liam Ryan, was the match-winner for St Kilda. AFL Photos via Getty Images



“Fingers crossed because if it is [serious], it’s so sad,” Hill said. “It’s been a tough journey for him the last couple of years, so I’m hoping nothing bad has happened.” King started every quarter on the bench and came on after the seven-minute mark each time. North Melbourne defenders Charlie Comben and Aidan Corr took turns playing on him, and rarely afforded him much space. His most notable impact was a forceful collision with Cam Zurhaar that cost the big Saint a 50-metre penalty after the Kangaroo reeled in an intercept mark. King’s nightmare period started with a season-ending posterior cruciate ligament tear in his left knee in a two-point loss to Port Adelaide at Marvel Stadium on June 30, 2024. Related Article AFL 2026 ‘Of course we can win it’: Defiant Dangerfield backs the Cats to contend again, despite his injury



He signed a six-year contract extension in October that year to tie him to the Saints until 2032, but has endured repeated injury complications since, including three surgeries on his right knee last year after a pre-season setback. King’s trouble continued with a calf injury in February before the hamstring strain in his second VFL match of the season in May delayed his return further. He spent part of his latest rehabilitation block on the Gold Coast, enabling him to spend time with his twin Ben, and St Kilda opted to bring him straight into the senior side. “It’s not ideal, right? But it’s about resilience and coming again,” Lyon said. “I think ultimately, you go, ‘Geez, I’ve run down the AFL race, I feel good, had a start, got a feel for how hard it is, and [I will] rehab a potential soft tissue’. Who knows what it is? I don’t know.



The Saints also lost Cooper Sharman (managed) and Rowan Marshall (back spasms) as late withdrawals, the latter after completing the warm-up. King could be facing another stint on the sidelines. AFL Photos via Getty Images Dashers Hill (34 disposals) and Darcy Wilson (28) were other prominent players for St Kilda, while ruckman Tom De Koning (19, seven clearances) shone in his return from broken ribs and a punctured lung. They led by 16 points at quarter-time – benefiting from a series of wayward North Melbourne set shots – but the Roos hit the front early in the second half via the second of Jack Darling’s three goals. But thanks to their 41-23 clearance dominance, the 10th-placed Saints hit back to lead by 13 points at the final break before kicking away for an important triumph.



Kangaroos defender Charlie Comben went to hospital after he was coughing up blood from a heavy collision late in the match, but coach Alastair Clarkson said the club’s doctors were optimistic he had avoided a serious issue.

World.title: ‘You idiot’: Piastri’s big blow-up as Hungarian Grand Prix unravels
World.content:
SportMotorsportFormula 1 ‘You idiot’: Piastri’s big blow-up as Hungarian Grand Prix unravels Hannah Kennelly July 27, 2026 — 2:45am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Oscar Piastri managed to have one of the best and worst races of his career on Sunday. His start was stupendous – getting past Ferrari’s Charles Leclerc and overtaking pole-sitter and teammate Lando Norris on the opening lap to lead the Hungarian Grand Pix. After a rough start to his 2026 campaign, it looked like this was finally Piastri’s moment, a legitimate chance for a grand prix win or a podium. Oscar Piastri has notched another DNF for his 2026 season. Clive Rose Piastri managed to hold Norris at bay for nearly half the race. Then it all went pear-shaped.



McLaren decided to pit Piastri on lap 34 and chose to keep Norris out to avoid Lewis Hamilton undercutting the McLarens. Piastri came into the pits, but was later caught behind back markers (slower cars that are about to be lapped) including Carlos Sainz, who clipped his front wheel. “Get out of the f---ing way, you idiot! Oh my God,” Piastri said over the radio. View post on X Moments later, Norris – who stayed longer on his second set of tyres – was able to pit and emerged in front of Piastri. The Australian’s race engineer informed Piastri over team radio that the collision with Sainz had cost him the lead of the race.



“Oh mate, just don’t **** talk to me now,” Piastri said in an uncharacteristic display of frustration. Piastri proceeded to criticise McLaren’s strategy, pointing out they put him in a situation where he would encounter traffic. “Nice of you guys to factor that one in by the way, thanks,” he said. View post on X On lap 56, Piastri’s McLaren spluttered to a halt on the side of the track, with a suspected gearbox failure. With 14 laps to go, his race was over and the Australian added another DNF to his resume.





The Australian star also had to deal with increasing rumours around the safety of his seat amid reports Verstappen is seeking an end to his Red Bull tenure. McLaren team principal Andrea Stella said it was good to see Norris and Piastri “fighting at the start for good position”, hailing it as “great racing”. Lando Norris won the Hungarian Grand Prix. Getty Images “Oscar had his own chance to take the lead and see what pace he might have had,” he told Sky Sports. “How the race unfolded meant that with Oscar we then covered Hamilton and then there was some situation with the backmarkers. Lando was very quick once he had the lead and he took advantage of the pace and the fact that there was some delay for Oscar.



“That’s racing. We are McLaren racing. It was great racing.” Speaking to media post-race, Piastri appeared more composed, and was his usual straightforward self. “I’m feeling pretty disappointed,” he said. “I feel like lap one was good, the first stint in general was reasonable and then struggled for pace on the hard ... but I had track position, and I felt like even though I was struggling, it felt like I could hang on, but from that point on, pretty much everything that could have gone wrong did. “On the strategy side, you don’t plan a strategy for getting taken out by a backmarker. So I can’t blame the team at all for that.
