World.title: Wildfires threaten Bordeaux as France, Spain battle blazes
World.content:
WorldEuropeExtreme weather Wildfires threaten Bordeaux as France, Spain battle blazes Manuel Ausloos and David Latona July 27, 2026 — 2:34am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Bordeaux/Madrid: Wildfires advanced toward the outskirts of the historic French city of Bordeaux at the heart of the country’s winelands on Sunday as France and Spain battled blazes that have already forced the evacuation of hundreds of thousands of people. About 220,000 people have been evacuated in France, while in Spain more than 75,000 people have had to leave their homes and around 30,000 more were ordered to shelter in place, authorities said. A firefighter battles a wildfire in San Martin de Valdeiglesias, west of Madrid, Spain, on Sunday. AP Photo/Manu Fernandez In France, fires have ravaged the Cap Ferret peninsula on the Atlantic coast, a popular tourist destination, and spread through areas surrounding Bordeaux, where firefighters were trying to prevent the flames from reaching the regional capital. “The fire is about 15 kilometres away from the entry points to the main city,” Bordeaux Mayor Thomas Cazenave said on Sunday, while Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said on X that the situation remained “difficult”.



Footage released by French police showed officers knocking on doors at night in the municipalities of Marcheprime and Cestas to evacuate homes one by one. Related Article Heatwave Europe’s summers are changing. The continent isn’t ready In Spain, Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez visited fire-hit areas in Avila, one of three central provinces affected by major blazes alongside Madrid and Toledo, where more than 45,000 hectares (111,000 acres) have burned. Spain battles multiple blazes A separate blaze in Spain’s eastern Castellon province has ravaged more than 4300 hectares, regional authorities said.



“The fire is out of control, it’s very difficult to extinguish from a technical standpoint, especially because of the adverse weather conditions that will continue throughout the day,” the regional leader of Valencia, Juanfran Perez, told reporters near the site. The wildfire has entered the Sierra de Espadan natural park, which contains large forests of pine trees and cork oaks. The fires are the latest disasters linked to prolonged drought and successive heatwaves that scientists say have been intensified by climate change. In both Bordeaux and Avila, July high temperatures have averaged 32 degrees Celsius, almost 6 degrees above the month’s normal high between 1961 and 1990, according to the Reuters Climate Monitor. International aid mobilised



Under the European Union’s civil protection mechanism, Greece and Italy have each sent two Canadair firefighting aircraft to Spain, while Portugal has deployed more than 100 military personnel along with equipment. Two more planes will arrive “as soon as possible” from Turkey, the Spanish interior ministry said on X. Loading Sanchez said his government would on Tuesday declare a civil protection emergency for the central provinces plagued by the wildfires, unlocking additional recovery funding. More than 150,000 hectares have burned across Spain since January, he said, six times the area destroyed during the same period last year.



While wildfires have long been a feature of Spain’s summers, Sanchez said their growing scale and intensity, fuelled by increasingly extreme weather, required policies grounded in climate science. More fires in Scotland, Italy In the highlands of Scotland, as many as 500 firefighters have been dealing with a large blaze within Cairngorms National Park since July 15. Residents of the village of Nethy Bridge, who were evacuated on Friday evening after a change in weather conditions, were allowed to return to their homes late on Saturday. A firefighter takes a break while battling a wildfire near Le Temple, outside Bordeaux. AP Photo/Emma Da Silva



A burnt vehicle sits outside a charred house in Navas del Rey, west of Madrid. AP Photo/Manu Fernandez In Italy, several bushfires forced the closure of a southern section of the Rome ring road as well as a motorway leading into the capital, causing major traffic disruption. In Italy’s southern Puglia region, tourists were evacuated from seaside resorts due to a large wildfire in the Gargano area, the national fire department said. Some were taken away by sea by the coast guard, the ANSA news agency added. Pope Leo, speaking from his summer residence of Castel Gandolfo outside Rome, offered spiritual support. “In light of the devastating wildfires that have affected various areas of France and Spain in recent days, I wish to express my solidarity and closeness, and I invite everyone to pray for those affected and for the rescue workers engaged in relief efforts,” he said.

World.title: ‘I’m sorry ... but’: Apologetic Alan Joyce tells his side of the Qantas story
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesAviation ‘I’m sorry ... but’: Apologetic Alan Joyce tells his side of the Qantas story Chris Zappone July 27, 2026 — 12:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Worse than the global financial crisis. Worse than the aftermath of the September 11 attacks. A shock to the industry that could cost the company 10,000 jobs. In 2020, these predictions of the damage COVID-19 would wreak on the aviation industry were ringing in the ears of the Qantas board and chief executive Alan Joyce when the “Flying Kangaroo” announced it would sack 1820 ground crew. The High Court later ruled the workers were sacked illegally and many are still waiting for compensation. Former Qantas chief executive Alan Joyce: “I apologise for the angst that was generated.” Louie Douvis It is only now, six years later – and three after stepping down as Qantas’ CEO – that Joyce has expressed some regret. His admission comes with caveats. Joyce says that if in August 2020, someone had told him “... on the other end of this there was going to be a vaccine, the vaccine was going to be effective, and that when the vaccine was going to work, there would be a massive rebound in demand – absolutely you would have made different decisions”.



“So with the information we had at the time, I still don’t think there was any other decision you could make,” he told this masthead during a video call from his Sydney home. “Hindsight is a great thing.” Speaking ahead of the launch of his book, Alan Joyce: Riding the Jet Stream, this week, Joyce said that despite his regrets, he cannot explain the post-lockdown resentment that continues to linger among the public. ‘I was the frog in the proverbial hot water and I didn’t know how hot it had gotten.’ Alan Joyce That’s perhaps not surprising from a man who, during his near 15-year tenure in the cockpit of Australia’s national airline, was not well known for his contrition. In moments of organisational chaos, political controversy and the “ghost flights” scandal, he was not prone to apology. Even now, the bottom line in Joyce’s mind was the bottom line of the company: Qantas survived COVID intact, and its shareholders didn’t lose a cent.



For Joyce, who spent an earlier portion of his career at Ansett Australia, keeping an airline alive is not academic. He had a front-row seat to Ansett’s collapse, having been its head of network planning when he left the company in 2000. It collapsed in 2001. Editor's pick Aviation Alan Joyce has been writing his book. Here’s how five people illegally sacked by his airline have fared “I’m actually very, very proud of the fact that I’m not sitting here and apologising for Qantas going bankrupt, [something] that many airlines around the world did,” Joyce says, pointing to the dozens of airlines around the world that went bankrupt, forced into mergers or put under administration during that period of time. That tally included Virgin Australia in 2020. “I think we would have caused more problems, more angst, if I was sitting here, and apologising for Qantas going bankrupt.” Qantas posted losses in 2021 and 2022 as COVID brought the business to a standstill, with an underlying loss before tax of $1.8 billion, only to swing decisively to a $2.4 billion profit in 2023 as public fury mounted over spiralling ticket prices and abysmal service outcomes. Joyce resigned two months early in September 2023.



Credit where it’s due Public anger compounded after the so-called “ghost flight” scandal, in which the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission fined Qantas $120 million for selling tickets for 8000 already cancelled flights. During COVID, Qantas appeared to bank up to $1.6 billion COVID travel credits that customers were unable to use amid mass flight cancellations triggered by border closures. The company did not clearly inform customers they were entitled to refunds. Under pressure, Qantas repeatedly extended the refund deadlines. It also agreed to a $105 million settlement following a class action against Qantas over the COVID-19 flight credits. Competitor Virgin, Joyce notes, just pocketed nearly $93 million because their credits expired. A Virgin spokesperson said: “More than 90 per cent of COVID credits were redeemed by guests”. Qantas has since removed all expiry dates and the outstanding amount remains on the balance sheet. The credits Qantas holds were worth $240 million as of December 31, 2025.



“I apologise for the angst that was generated [for] the customers on it, but the reality was we had 22 million bookings in the system [and] the system wasn’t designed to do an automatic refund,” he said. On many of Joyce or the airline’s most notable public controversies, his responses follow this familiar formula: “I’m sorry, but … “We were trying to fix things on the go, but it got a lot better as we went through it... Eventually, we got there and probably had the best policy of any airline out there,” he says. ‘Part of the job’ Few in corporate Australia have faced scrutiny or public pressure in the way Joyce did, particularly through the latter stages of his tenure. At Qantas, he says, they joked about the “Himalayas of brand reporting,” referring to the drastic peaks and troughs of consumer sentiment.



Joyce faced white-hot anger from airline customers during his time at the helm. In 2024, a best-selling book by journalist Joe Aston probing the company’s dealings with politicians captured public attention. Some singled him out over the airline’s stance on social issues. Joyce, now happily married to his long-term partner Shane Lloyd, was criticised for the organisation’s support of the “Yes” campaign for marriage equality in 2017. Two-thirds of Australians voted supporting the campaign, but that didn’t stop a protester smashing a pie into Joyce’s face while he spoke on stage at a Perth event. When senior Coalition politician Peter Dutton criticised a group of CEOs who signed a letter supporting the campaign, Joyce was the one he singled out. Joyce endured attacks and criticism over the company’s position on social issues. That aside, Joyce doesn’t see himself as a victim, or a fall guy for post-lockdown resentment. He accepts “because it was part of the job”, the bouts of extreme criticism he was at times subjected to. He also laments what he describes as the reluctance of corporate leaders to advocate on political and social issues as Qantas did in 2017 and in 2023, when the company supported the unsuccessful referendum campaign for an Indigenous Voice to parliament.



“I think there’s obviously fewer people doing it, if any, and I think that’s a shame because I think corporations are part of society,” he says. Editor's pick Updated

Aviation Qantas to pay $105m after class action over cancelled COVID flights On whether broader societal discontent in the post-COVID years played a role in the criticism, he said: “I really can’t answer that because I certainly don’t have any post-lockdown resentment.” “Maybe some people in the community do, but I certainly don’t.” Of Aston’s book, The Chairman’s Lounge, Joyce denied its claim he upgraded Prime Minister Anthony Albanese’s son to the lounge, an invitation-only club usually reserved for politicians and business leaders.



The book also alleged Joyce arranged flight upgrades for the prime minister and senior politicians. He said others in the company had the ability to arrange upgrades. “I do not remember him ever ringing me asking for an upgrade. I had to get my PA to do it on a computer … I rang her when the claim came out,” he says. “She said she had no memory of ever doing it for me. Anytime I did an upgrade I signed a document. I believe the documentation was checked and there’s no document for me signing.” Prime Minister Anthony Albanese with former Qantas chief executive Alan Joyce in 2023. AAP The exit lounge Ultimately, Joyce’s legacy echoes at higher volume within the aviation industry than it does in the public arena or political circles.



When Joyce stepped down as CEO, trust in the Qantas brand was at a low ebb and his replacement, Vanessa Hudson, who was chief financial officer under Joyce, is seeking to rebuild it. Other parts of his handover were brighter. Budget subsidiary Jetstar, of which Joyce was the founding CEO, remains profitable and has announced a slew of new routes despite rising fuel costs. Project Sunrise, a Joyce brainchild to connect Sydney to London non-stop appears to be on track for the first flights to begin next year, with the specially adapted Airbus A350 having visited Melbourne last week. Internationally, Joyce remains a respected voice in global aviation, having served as chairman of the oneworld governing board, as well as chairman of the board of governors for the International Air Transport Association. It wasn’t until his first year after leaving, while decompressing from 15 years as CEO, that he realised the full extent of the high-pressure situation he was in during his twilight months in the role. “I was the frog in the proverbial hot water and I didn’t know how hot it had gotten,” he says.



He spent that year enjoying a quieter life with husband Shane and travelled back to Ireland to look after his mother. Joyce was later persuaded to write the book, which he described as a “cathartic experience”. Loading Uncertain future Asked about the impact of the unfolding Middle East conflict on global aviation, Joyce said the situation could go either way and executives would be preparing for a wide range of scenarios – everything from another ceasefire and a return to normal (in which case oil prices drop and demand surges). Or the conflict could widen to the point that not just the Persian Gulf is closed, but also the Red Sea. If so, that’s when “you get into really bad territory for airlines”.



Joyce, who studied physics and mathematics at the Dublin Institute of Technology and later studied at Trinity College, said airlines would be examining the probability of each scenario. If the conflict paralyses oil shipments, “it doesn’t matter how much you’re willing to pay, you just don’t get supply”. That situation would be something akin to “COVID without the masks”, Joyce said, and flights would be grounded again. After reading Joyce’s book and listening to him discuss his career at length, one can have no doubt that if he was still in charge of an airline navigating the challenges coming out of the Middle East, there would be no question about his approach. He would listen to the experts and take whatever action he thought necessary to protect the company, however drastic, no matter the personal cost. And he wouldn’t apologise for it. World.title: Extraordinary meeting of Labor conveners resolves to move against Jacinta Allan
World.content:
An internal Labor Party campaign to dump Jacinta Allan as Victorian premier reached a critical stage on Sunday night after an extraordinary meeting of factional conveners resolved to move against her leadership. The meeting of conveners from across the party’s Left and Right factions was called to determine whether Allan has the caucus backing she needs to lead the government to the state election on November 28. Four sources with knowledge of the meeting said the room broadly agreed that after nearly three years as Premier, Allan’s days in the top job are numbered. It is less clear how a leadership challenge will unfold. A meeting of factional conveners on Sunday night resolved to dump Jacinta Allan as the leader of Victorian Labor. Michael Howard One source told The Age that the premier had been informed on Sunday night that she had lost the support of the Labor caucus.



A defiant Allan, who spent Sunday night at her home in Bendigo with senior advisers, told her supporters that, regardless of what the factional chiefs decide, she would not resign. The leadership manoeuvres are taking place in the absence of a declared challenger. Allan’s most likely replacement, Deputy Premier Ben Carroll, has indicated to colleagues that while he would be a contender if the leadership became vacant, he would not use his numbers to bring the premier down. Deputy Premier Ben Carroll has been touted as Allan’s most likely replacement. Alex Coppel A contested leadership ballot, just four months out from a state election, would paralyse the government.



Under previously untested party rules, a new leader would be chosen by a caucus vote and ballot of party members, with even weight given to both. The process can take up to six weeks. In the event of a leadership spill, the deputy leader steps in to run the government. If Allan and Carroll are leadership candidates, both would be sidelined from their day jobs and an interim leader appointed. There is consternation among some MPs, particularly in the dominant Left faction, that the factional conveners did not sufficiently canvass the views of parliamentarians within their respective groups before Sunday night’s meeting. The Age has spoken to seven Victorian Labor sources who say they believe Allan would lose if her leadership came to a vote of the party’s 69 MPs. But one MP told The Age not every faction was represented at the Sunday night meeting and downplayed its significance.



“The premier absolutely has the numbers,” they said. “Some people don’t want to do the hard work. They want things on a plate and I can tell you now the caucus are there behind the premier.” As with the last round of leadership rumblings in June, the pathway for a coup is littered with assumptions that have not yet been realised. Multiple sources from both factions agreed it would be difficult for Carroll, who sits on the Right, to challenge Allan – despite some within her own Left faction wanting him to do so – after he publicly ruled out a challenge at a press conference last month. After looking the premier in the eye and declaring he would not challenge her for the leadership, Carroll told reporters, “I’ve got a young daughter at home, and I couldn’t be more proud to make sure that she grows up knowing that I supported Jacinta Allan to be a world-class premier and get re-elected in her own right.”



Another option being considered is a delegation of factional leaders speaking to Allan and asking her to step aside. Two sources said they found it difficult to believe Allan would go down without a fight, but conceded it was not impossible that she could be convinced if it were clear she no longer had the numbers in caucus. A supporter of Allan, speaking on the condition of anonymity to talk freely, said if the Sunday night meeting showed a majority of MPs wanted a change of leadership, the premier could face a vote of no confidence at Tuesday’s caucus meeting. “It would be a very brave premier that continued in light of an unfavourable outcome,” they said.



Attorney-General Sonya Kilkenny, speaking earlier on Sunday, said the leadership speculation was “idle gossip”. Related Article Exclusive

Victorian election Revealed: Secret government plan to tackle organised crime “She has my full support, and this idle gossip doesn’t help Victorians,” she said. “It is only hurting Victorians at a time when Victorians need us all to be focused on them, and that is exactly what Jacinta Allan and our Labor government, our team, is doing.” Over the past week, a range of new policies have leaked from the Premier’s Private Office that suggest Allan’s team is trying to find announcements that could mollify her colleagues. On Monday, cabinet will consider a proposal to create a new agency within Victoria Police that targets organised crime and is informed by Australia’s best criminal intelligence.



The policy has been viewed internally as a way to kill off pressure for a royal commission into Big Build corruption, tying the issue together with other political problems such as an increase in firebombings in Melbourne, and community concerns about youth crime rates. Another leaked policy floated amending the rate cap rules to allow councils to better recoup the costs needed to pay staff – a policy supported by the Australian Services Union but quickly seized on by the opposition as a cost-of-living attack. One MP said Allan was in denial about her support and rather than step aside would likely enforce party rules for a spill, which requires a vote of the Labor membership if the caucus result is contested. But they also said those conspiring needed to “piss or get off the pot”. A senior Labor figure said Allan’s leadership had been doomed, and she was now incredibly unpopular despite being given time to connect with voters.



Related Article Analysis

Building Bad Nobody measures ‘Bandidos kickbacks’: How construction costs took CFMEU centre stage “There is now an opportunity to push the reset button, give confidence back to voters and remind voters of the benefits of a strong Labor government.” The latest Resolve Political Monitor has Allan’s likeability at minus 36, her equal lowest result on record. Opposition Leader Jess Wilson maintains a lead on preferred premier, with 43 per cent of voters saying they want her to lead the state compared with 24 per cent for Allan. More Victorian politics:

World.title: Markel ado about nothing? The verdict on Meghan as guest MasterChef judge
World.content:
FoodMasterChef Recap Markel ado about nothing? The verdict on Meghan as guest MasterChef judge The Duchess of Sussex makes her much-hyped appearance on MasterChef and shares her not-so-famous home cooking expertise with the giddy amateur cooks. Ben Pobjie July 26, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

And so it came to pass, that Meghan Duchess of Sussex arrived at the MasterChef kitchen, and just like Poochie the Dog, she made life worthwhile for us all. And what a spectacular entrance it was. After Poh gives her a grand and really quite misleading introduction – describing her as a “global icon” and someone known for her “home cooking”, so that nobody could possibly guess who it might be – the woman herself walks down the red carpet to widespread bafflement. Meghan and her impressive table of produce under the chandeliers. Channel Ten/Kelly Gardner As well as the final four amateur cooks, all eliminated contestants were allowed to be in the room to witness the royal event, and every one of them performs impressive impressions of people who are impressed. The sense that Meghan’s presence in the kitchen is utterly inexplicable, however, is impossible to miss – if Robert Irwin as a guest judge was confusing, this is bewilderment on a scale rarely seen on Australian television since the demise of It’s A Knockout. Many people might have questioned the Duchess’s credentials as a cooking expert, but those people are immediately shut up when she revealed a table full of fruits and vegetables and demonstrates that she knows all their names and how to pronounce them properly (as opposed to the word “herb”, which she pronounces wrongly because she is American).



Meghan, Duchess of Sussex on the set of MasterChef Australia Channel 10/Supplied Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up “Your time starts now,” she announces, showing all the acting chops she honed on Suits, as she plays the part of a person who has the slightest interest in anyone else in the room. As the cooks rush to make their dishes – the task was to take an ingredient and make a meal “fit for a duchess”, or more specifically fit for a duchess who has been excluded from the royal family – the judges surround Meghan to tell her how wonderful she is and ask her what she would cook and how she got to be so beautiful and what brand of shampoo she uses. The cooks themselves come up with all kinds of crazy concepts, but we wouldn’t want to dwell on those. As the old TV industry aphorism goes, if you want people to pay attention to the food, you do not get Meghan on as a guest judge. It is notable, however, that Aaron appears to have a crush on Meghan and is quite flustered when talking to her about carrots. Incidentally, carrots are one of the many vegetables that Meghan ABSOLUTELY LOVES. Petro makes celeriac ice-cream, in line with his well-earned reputation as “guy who makes desserts out of ludicrous things”. And it was a wise choice for the guest judge too, because Meghan LOVES celeriac. And she LOVES the idea of celeriac ice-cream. And she LOVES being on television. Neither Petro nor Aaron can believe they are cooking for Meghan, who, to be clear, is not just an ordinary human being: she is an ordinary human being who married someone very famous. As such she makes all those other guest judges who have achieved massive success in food by their talent and years of hard work really look like pathetic losers.



Meghan LOVES celeriac. And she LOVES the idea of celeriac ice-cream. And she LOVES being on television. At one point, Poh drags Meghan over to a table and makes her eat her banana and date loaf, just so they can say the duchess really earned her fee. Meghan asks Poh if she can have the recipe and Poh says she can, both knowing that in an hour or so they will part ways and never talk to each other again for the rest of their lives. There is also some cooking going on – Vinnie, like Petro, is using celeriac, but unlike Petro is being normal and not making ice-cream out of it. Instead he is cooking a steak and draping celeriac in decorative ways over it. Meghan is SO EXCITED about this. Meanwhile, Casper has an artichoke. “That artichoke looks wild!” shout the watchers from the balcony, where they’re really starved of things to get excited about now they’ve all talked about how INSANE and CRAZY and UNBELIEVABLE it is to have Meghan here. Quickly we cut away from the cooking to listen to Meghan talk about her show, With Love, Meghan, which is just like MasterChef apparently because it’s all about “cooking for joy”. Also, just like MasterChef contestants, Meghan has no qualifications or experience as a professional cook, so there are a lot of parallels.



But you can’t deny that she’s got a real knack for walking up to people and telling them there’s 30 minutes left. So good at this is she, in fact, that after she tells all four contestants, everyone gives her a round of applause. And why not? They just watched a woman walk around a room without falling over and say several words – not everyone can do this! “It feels like she’s looking into your soul,” says Casper, possibly hinting that Meghan might secretly be a demon? This is backed up when he immediately cuts himself for the first time this season. The Duchess’s powers are indeed terrifying, as the blood flows in the kitchen. Casper has a vision for cooking octopus, and Meghan LOVES that. “Make it sparkle for Meghan Markle!” Sofia shouts, and doggone it that is just about the most brilliant bit of wordplay anyone present has ever heard. The kitchen practically explodes with happiness. Shortly after this, Petro says a sequence of words that has never been spoken before in human history: “My concern with the ice-cream is that there might not be enough celeriac.” So this episode is historic for two reasons. Meghan then tastes Petro’s ice-cream and immediately assumes an expression of intense distress, as if she’s just been forced to watch a dog being strangled. It is a moment of high panic as Petro contemplates the likelihood that he is about to serve the worst plate of food ever made to an actual duchess/fictional lawyer. But he still has time to try to make it taste non-horrible. It’s celeriac ice-cream so he probably can’t, but he can try.



Judges Jean Christophe Novelli looking cranky, Poh Ling Yeow, Meghan and Sofia Levin. Ten The judging process is incredibly tense: Casper’s octopus, Vinnie’s steak, Petro’s ice-cream and Aaron’s stir-fry must compete not only against each other, but also against the impossibly refined palate of Meghan Markle, Ethereal Super-Being. There’s also tension emanating from Jean-Christophe, who’s looked pissed off for the whole episode, as if he’s itching to ask Meghan how many Michelin stars she’s got. But the Duchess comes through with some truly penetrating insights into the food she eats, like “I love this dish” and “It’s so good”. You can definitely see how she became a Duchess, a title traditionally granted only to the most discerning of reality TV cooking judges. The most amazing part of the judging is when a producer suddenly walks into shot and hands Meghan a phone, on which Prince Harry himself is Facetiming! Isn’t that amazing? Just on the spur of the moment it happened! I’ve never seen anything so spontaneous and unplanned! Everyone again bursts into applause for the concept of unearned privilege. Anyway in the end everyone loves every dish, even Petro’s psychotic ice-cream. In fact, it’s the dish of the day and Petro goes through to the semi-final, proving the ironclad rule of MasterChef: put something stupid in ice-cream and you’ll win. The judges thank Meghan for coming all this way just to earn a large amount of money and promote her brand, and everyone is happy, especially Meghan, who now gets to go to her hotel room and forget about it. As for the rest of us, we can only sit back, spent, and wonder, as a civilisation, what we have wrought. Related Article Opinion So, Meghan’s going on MasterChef? Our resident show expert shares his thoughts Ben Pobjie Entertainment writer

World.title: ‘We stand by our decision to play him’: Lyon feels the heat after King’s AFL comeback ends early
World.content:
Updated SportAFLAFL 2026 ‘We stand by our decision to play him’: Lyon feels the heat after King’s AFL comeback ends early Marc McGowan Updated July 26, 2026 — 9:48pm ,first published 5:29pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

St Kilda coach Ross Lyon is adamant tortured St Kilda spearhead Max King was ready to play on Sunday despite his first AFL game in 757 days ending prematurely due to hamstring tightness. King’s latest setback in a challenging period for the 26-year-old marred the Saints’ 31-point win over fellow wildcard contender North Melbourne at Marvel Stadium, including a four-goal-to-one final quarter that transformed a competitive contest into a comfortable victory. Max King in full flight during Sunday’s match. AFL Photos via Getty Images Resident superstar Nasiah Wanganeen-Milera was the difference again, kicking three of his four goals after going forward in the third quarter as part of a 46-disposal performance that ripped the match away from the Kangaroos. Lyon did not speak to King before his post-game media conference, but said that the star forward would undergo scans on Monday to assess any potential damage. The coach backed his medical staff’s decision to give King the green light after he suffered a hamstring strain in a VFL game in May.



Related Article Investigation

AFL off-field behaviour Crime threats, nude pics and a Tinder date: Inside the AFL’s most secretive unit “I don’t even know what the outcome is, so how can it be an error before there’s an outcome?” Lyon said. “But we stand by our decision to play him. We have high-performance experts, we have [training] load, we have conditioning. We’re really quite confident. “In the four-week [rehabilitation] block, he had 50 per cent more volume of high-speed running, and 500 per cent more very high-speed running, which is above 24 kilometres [an hour]. His biggest sessions were game-load sessions with 20 per cent more. “So, in the context of that evidence, our conditioners thought [he was ready], and game time was only 12 minutes a quarter – two six-minute stints. It was very considered, very worked out, and I’m happy for it to sit with me and our team because we collaborate.”



King had just one kick – a long set shot from the boundary in the second quarter – and one handball in limited game time, but left the ground for good only 13 minutes into the third term. He went to the rooms soon after and did not reappear before the Saints ruled him out. King’s hamstring strain in May added to the knee and calf setbacks which stalled a promising career that was stuck on 83 games for more than two years. Speaking post-match to SEN, St Kilda veteran Brad Hill was hopeful King had avoided another lengthy lay-off. Nasiah Wanganeen-Milera, being embraced by teammate Liam Ryan, was the match-winner for St Kilda. AFL Photos via Getty Images



“Fingers crossed because if it is [serious], it’s so sad,” Hill said. “It’s been a tough journey for him the last couple of years, so I’m hoping nothing bad has happened.” King started every quarter on the bench and came on after the seven-minute mark each time. North Melbourne defenders Charlie Comben and Aidan Corr took turns playing on him, and rarely afforded him much space. His most notable impact was a forceful collision with Cam Zurhaar that cost the big Saint a 50-metre penalty after the Kangaroo reeled in an intercept mark. King’s nightmare period started with a season-ending posterior cruciate ligament tear in his left knee in a two-point loss to Port Adelaide at Marvel Stadium on June 30, 2024. Related Article AFL 2026 ‘Of course we can win it’: Defiant Dangerfield backs the Cats to contend again, despite his injury



He signed a six-year contract extension in October that year to tie him to the Saints until 2032, but has endured repeated injury complications since, including three surgeries on his right knee last year after a pre-season setback. King’s trouble continued with a calf injury in February before the hamstring strain in his second VFL match of the season in May delayed his return further. He spent part of his latest rehabilitation block on the Gold Coast, enabling him to spend time with his twin Ben, and St Kilda opted to bring him straight into the senior side. “It’s not ideal, right? But it’s about resilience and coming again,” Lyon said. “I think ultimately, you go, ‘Geez, I’ve run down the AFL race, I feel good, had a start, got a feel for how hard it is, and [I will] rehab a potential soft tissue’. Who knows what it is? I don’t know.



The Saints also lost Cooper Sharman (managed) and Rowan Marshall (back spasms) as late withdrawals, the latter after completing the warm-up. King could be facing another stint on the sidelines. AFL Photos via Getty Images Dashers Hill (34 disposals) and Darcy Wilson (28) were other prominent players for St Kilda, while ruckman Tom De Koning (19, seven clearances) shone in his return from broken ribs and a punctured lung. They led by 16 points at quarter-time – benefiting from a series of wayward North Melbourne set shots – but the Roos hit the front early in the second half via the second of Jack Darling’s three goals. But thanks to their 41-23 clearance dominance, the 10th-placed Saints hit back to lead by 13 points at the final break before kicking away for an important triumph.



Kangaroos defender Charlie Comben went to hospital after he was coughing up blood from a heavy collision late in the match, but coach Alastair Clarkson said the club’s doctors were optimistic he had avoided a serious issue.

World.title: Commonwealth Games: Worn-out Hamish Kerr withdraws from Glasgow high jump
World.content:
New Zealand high jumper Hamish Kerr has officially withdrawn from this year's Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, due to burnout.

The Olympic and world champion was last month named among the 21 track and field athletes for the Games, which started on Friday, despite not competing internationally this season.

Kerr sparked doubt over his Games prospects earlier this month in a social media post, explaining the demands of the last few months had caught up with him, and that he was taking a break from training.

At the time, Athletics New Zealand said the 29-year-old would be at the Games, but a decision on whether he contests the high jump would be made "closer to the time".

The defending Commonwealth Games champion had been due to compete in the men's high jump final on Tuesday morning( NZT), but confirmed overnight he would not be competing.

"The start of this year, had a massive few years, felt like the body was good and ready to get training, but we realised pretty quickly I was pretty burnt out," he told reporters in Glasgow.

"Took a bit of a step back and had a nice physical mental reset just over the last couple of months."

Kerr had resumed training and said he was happy with the progress he was making.

"I'm just not quite ready and not in a position that I want to be to go out there, and do the singlet and the New Zealand team justice.

Hamish Kerr addresses media at the Glasgow Commonwealth Games. RNZ / Adam Burns

"Unfortunate to make the decision and it was one that was not made lightly," he said. "I'm super excited to support the rest of the team - not just athletics, but the wider team - and be here for the week, and get behind the New Zealand team."

High Performance New Zealand had worked closely with Kerr on his physical and mental wellbeing.

Kerr had hoped, by arriving in Glasgow, he would be "ready to go".

"Just over the last few days, I've realised that there's probably still a little bit of work to do and we will continue to do that in the next few weeks."

After winning gold at the 2024 Paris Olympics, Kerr said he still had his sights on defending his Olympic title in Los Angeles in two years.

"That is certainly the intention and that is the reasoning behind the time that this has taken.

"I think that's important this year to explore these things and really make sure that I'm right for the bigger ones coming forward."

When asked if he would be competing again this season, Kerr replied "maybe".

Since winning gold at the last Commonwealth Games in 2022, Kerr has won an indoor world champion title, become an Olympic champion and won gold at the world athletics championships.

World.title: National promises to extend paid parental leave from 26 weeks to 30, if re-elected
World.content:
National has pledged to extend paid parental leave from 26 weeks to 30, if re-elected.

The party is also proposing to revive a policy that allows parents to take some or all of their leave at the same time.

Since 2020, primary carers have been eligible for 26 weeks of paid leave and an additional 26 weeks of unpaid leave.

National has proposed changing the entitlement incrementally, increasing it to 27 weeks in 2027, 28 weeks in 2028, and then 30 weeks in 2029.

Finance spokesperson Nicola Willis said the policy modernised paid parental leave, supporting families to give them more financial breathing space while they took on caregiving responsibilities.

"The birth of a child is an expensive time, as families juggle the costs that come with a new baby while their household income is less than when both parents are in paid work," she said.

Nicola Willis at the announcement on Sunday. TU NATANAHIRA / RNZ

"Extending paid parental leave to 30 weeks will ease that pressure and give more parents the option to stay home with their baby for longer."

Leave is currently capped at $811 a week. National's policy did not propose an increase to that, but Willis said the government had increased the cap each year.

National is also bringing back a previous policy that would allow parents to split their leave.

Christopher Luxon speaking to a child at the announcement. TU NATANAHIRA / RNZ

The party used an example of instead of one parent taking 30 weeks' leave, both parents could take 15 weeks together, or both parents could take 4 weeks together, then one parent could take 10 weeks, and then the other parent could take 12 weeks.

Willis said the current law was restrictive and got in the way of families doing what they thought was best for their babies.

"Whether a dad wants to support mum in the first few weeks after birth, or two caregivers want to share paid leave in overlapping instalments, the choice should sit with families and not restricted by outdated government rules."

The policy would be funded out of Budget operating allowances, costing $27 million in 2027/28, $56.6m in 2028/29, and $119m in 2029/30.

That larger extension is timed to coincide with the forecast return to surplus.

National claims its long-term intention is to increase the entitlement to 40 weeks, but it has not put a timeframe on when it would want to achieve this.

The policy announcement comes as National MPs rally around their colleague Katie Nimon.

The Napier MP's would-be challenger, Stuart Nash, resigned as a New Zealand First candidate, after coming under fire for labelling Nimon as lazy for taking nine months off after having a baby.

MPs do not get paid parental leave. Nimon confirmed she took ten weeks of parental leave and returned to Parliament after six months.

Nimon, who was present at the press conference, said Nash called her on Thursday to apologise.

"He just offered his apology for offending me," she said.

The party insisted it had not timed the announcement off the back of the saga, but Nimon said her views on the policy would be the same regardless of recent events.

"I've said a lot this week, there is no right way of being a working parent. We just need to give people the choice. This policy that we're putting forward is really going to give people that choice. I stand by that, whether what happened this week happened or not."

In 2023, Willis proposed allowing parents to share their leave entitlement so they could take time off together. The member's bill was voted down by Labour at first reading.

Labour then went on to campaign for four weeks' paid parental leave for partners.

National had put forward a member's bill this term to allow for split parental leave, in the name of East Coast MP Dana Kirkpatrick.

It had been unable to get the changes into the coalition agreement or pass them as a government this term. Willis said the responsibility for parental leave rested with the Workplace Relations and Safety Minister, ACT's Brooke van Velden.

"I think it's a shame that it wasn't prioritised within the minister's programme for this term, and we are really keen as a National Party to see this done."

ACT leader David Seymour defended his colleague, saying van Velden had not worked on parental leave flexibility because she had not been asked to.

"She hasn't been asked by the National Party to do that. It's not in their coalition documents. They didn't try and negotiate it into their agreement. I was disappointed because I think people want to see the coalition pointing to what it's achieved rather than pointing fingers at each other."

Seymour said the timing of the announcement felt political, given the events of the past week.

Labour leader Chris Hipkins asked why National should be trusted now.

"They have had three years to make life easier for Kiwis and support families, but have instead cut Best Start support for parents, reduced funding for school lunches, cut women's pay, and failed to tackle the cost of living."

Hipkins said Labour would have a "comprehensive" paid parental leave policy, which it would set out in due course.

Green Party co-leader Marama Davidson said National's policy was too little, too late.

"The only time that government cares about women is when it is polling low. We have seen them trash the lives of women, whether it's through cancelling pay equity claims for hundreds of thousands of women, whether it's in keeping wage growth low, because that impacts disproportionately women. This government made decisions to keep one in seven children in poverty. That is, children and their mothers."

Last month, National announced a policy to continue paying the government KiwiSaver contribution to people on paid parental leave.

Some parents online called National's promise to extend paid parental leave a "lolly scramble".

Many questioned why National would wait until after an election to implement much needed help, and more said the policy was not enough.

A few commenters on Facebook suggested that increasing the payments rather than the length of the leave would help families more.

A couple said they had had to go to work earlier because they could not afford to live on PPL payments.

Lisa, Wellington mum of a two-and-a-half-year old, said the policy was a step in the right direction but was missing the bigger issue: the cost of early childhood education (ECE).

"I know parents that are paying upwards of $1500 a fortnight for two children just to keep their jobs, or else they're just opting to leave their careers," she said.

She said help with childcare costs would have left her better off financially than more time off work.

"We constantly hear Christopher Luxon saying he wants to get people back to work, but you're getting people back to work who are then having to spend half their salary on ECE fees just so they can go to work. It's just this awful cycle."

She said the high fees were also keeping people from having more children.

World.title: Commonwealth Games: Silver Ferns face Jamaica in crucial netball pool game
World.content:
New Zealand face an early test of their Commonwealth Games medal prospects, when they take on Jamaica in pool play at Glasgow.

The Silver Ferns ran out convincing 74-44 winners over hosts Scotland in their opening game and the OVO Hydro, but the 'Calypso Queens' present a much tougher challenge, with only two teams progressing from each pool to the semifinals.

Jamaica took silver at Birmingham four years ago, defeating the Kiwis 67-51 in the semis, and overcame the Ferns 60-55 for bronze at Gold Coast 2018.

They opened their Glasgow account with an 81-22 win over Trinidad & Tobago.

Elsewhere, swimmer Hazel Ouwehand - bronze medallist over 50m butterfly - will race the same stroke over 100 metres. The NZ men face Cayman Islands and Scotland, with a 3x3 basketball semifinal spot at stake, while gymnasts Daniel Stoddart and Courtney McGregor contest the individual all-round finals.

Kiwis are also active at boxing and bowls.

World.title: Commonwealth Games: Pacific hope for medals in bowls and boxing
World.content:
There is hope that the Pacific Island contingent at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow will be able to win medals in bowling and boxing.

Top Fijii men's singles player Rajnesh Parasad is the best bet for a medal in the bowls, following his early three round wins so far.

Prasad claimed his first win on Friday morning, when he beat England's top bowler Sam Tolchard in a tie-break, after the two players were tied 1-1 at the end of two sets.

Tolchard won the prestigious World Singles Champion of Champions title in November 2022 in New Zealand, and claimed the top title at the Bowls World Cup in November 2025.

Prasad then defeated Jamaica's Robert Simpson 2-0 in clean sets in his second game. He won 12-1 in the first and 6-5 in the second to wrap the game up.

He also claimed his third win on Sunday morning, taking the tie-break against Scotland's Jason Banks, after the duo had ended the game tied with a set each to their names.

In boxing, male boxers Kiribati's Eriu Temakau won his men's 55kg bout in a split-points decisions against Guernsey's Thomas Teers.

Papua New Guinea's James Paul also got through his first fight, winning a points decision as well over Bahrains Rashield Williams.

Tonga's Josh Tonga is the third Pasifika boxer to win his first bout, defeating Trinidad and Tobago's Jeremiah Thomas in the men's 80kg division.

The three Pasifika boxers will feature in the Round of 16.

Tonga told the media after his win he was excited and looks forward to his next bout.

"Amazing," he said.

"Words can't explain, the atmosphere is insane, and our team is behind me, coaches, families and friends watching as well, it's incredible.

"The game plan was to keep my distance, take little wee steps, keeping it simple in general."

In other results:

Bowls - Women's Pairs

Norfolk Islands pair of Ellie Dixon and Christie Jones beat Cook Islands duo Fa'amanatu Vasie Ngatoko-Oila and Teokotai Rahui Jim 2-0, winning 8-3 and 10-1 in both sets.

Cook Islands returned strong in the second game of the weekend, when they defeated Falkland Islands 2-0, winning 8-2 and 8-2 in the two sets.

Norfolk Islands also did the same when they beat the Jersey pair 2-0 in their clash, winning 7-1 and 7-2..

Niue's Catherine Papani and Christine Ioane lost 2-0 to the Northern Ireland pair of Chloe Wilson and Shauna O'Neill. Northern Ireland won both sets 9-1 and 11-0.

They also lost 2-0 to Singapore, losing both sets 12-4 and 11-2 and went down to Zambia as well.

The Tonga pair of paris Baker and Milika Nathan dropped game two after their first round win, this time losing on tie-break to England. The two teams battled to winning a set each before England took the tie-break 1-0.

They also lost their third game, going down too on tie-break to India in another tight game.

Fijian pair Litia Tikoisuva and Losalini Tukai went down 2-0 to Wales in their second game. Wales won both sets 8-0 amd 5-3.

They did win their next game, beating Kenya 1.5-0.5, claiming the first set 7-2 before the two teams fought to a 5-all draw in the second set.

Bowls - Men's Singles

Royden Aperau of Cook Islands defeated Taylor Greechan of Jersey in a tie-break. Greechan won the first set 5-4 before Aperau claimed the second 9-2 and then won the tie-break 2-0.

He was unlcuky on Sunday morning when he lost 2-0 to Isle of Man's Mark McGreal.

But then came back strong to win 2-0 against Guernsey's Jason Greenslade.

Tonga's Liam Hall won two games after having lost in the first round, defeating Niue's Frederrick Tafatu 2-0. Hall won 11-4 and 8-4 to secure a clean record in that game.

He then defeated South Africa's Wayne Rittmuller in his third game, taking the tie-break in that clash.

Niue's Tafatu, on the other hand, took New Zealand's Shannon McIlroy to the wire in their match before losing on tie-break, after both players had claimed a set each in normal play.

However, he lost to Northern Ireland's Gary Kelly in the tie-break when the two had fought to winning a set each. Kelly took the tie-break 1-0 to claim victory.

Boxing

Fiji's Ben Maukakala lost his first fight and exited the Games after the referee stopped the contest in round two of his men's 65kg clash against New Zealand's Connor Campbell.

Nauru's Vi-J Tebouwa also suffered a loss against Scotland's Leo Church in his opening bout of the same division.

However, not all was good for Vanuatu's Ricksen Nomleas who lost in the first round against England's Ellis Trowbridge and Solomon Islands' Clinton Tetekana, who lost to Bangladesh's Md Rakib Hossan. Both Nomleas and Tetekana were saved by the referee who stpped in to stop their fights.

PNG's Petronella Nokenoke lost by points to England's Lucy Kings-Wheatley in the women's 60kg contest.

On Sunday morning, mixed results were again recorded by Pasifika boxers.

Niue's Phoenix Gataua lost on points to Botswana's Treasure Moremi, followed by loses also to Solomon Islands duo Lio Dicks and Max Makana, Fiji's Jone Davule, Niue's Kalani Anitelea-Launiu and Samoa's Dee Ioapo.

3x3 Basketball

In the women's competition, Fiji defeated Cayman Islands 16-6 in their opening Pool A game but lost 16-14 to Kenya in their second match and Australia 21-3 in their third game.

Tonga beat Scotland 12-10 in their Pool B opener and Papua New Guinea in their third game, but lost 21-8 to New Zealand in their second match.

PNG lost 22-6 to New Zealand and 21-8 to Singapore as well in their Pool G games.

In the men's competition, the Fiji men's team lost 21-16 to Malaysia, 21-13 to England but beat Jamaica 21-13 in their three Pool B games.

The Games media said there was a lovely moment from Tongan sisters Mele Finau and Lesila Finau, who helped the Pacific nation to a surprise 12-10 win over hosts Scotland in their opening match of the Women's 3x3 Basketball, with younger sibling Mele saying:

"She has been my role model for the past 20-something years. It has been great having her by my side and representing our country together. Sibling love can be a bit of tough love at times but it definitely helps on the court."

Swimming

Cook Islands' Carter Makira finished sixth in the heat two of the men's 200 metres individual medley, while Samoa's Christian Toia was eighth in heat three.

Nafanua Hamilton was placed sixth in the women's 200m backstroke heats. She also placed eigth in the women's 200m freestyle.

In the women's 50 metres butterfly heats PNG pair Jhnayali Tokome-Garap and Roxanne Kirarock finished third and fourth respectively in heat one, while teammate Joanna Chew was fourth in heat two, ahead of Vanuatu's Loane Russet, who was at fifth spot.

Fiji's Anahira McCutcheon finished fourth in heat five, while Samoa's Paige Schendelaar-Kemp was eighth in that heat.

PNG's Thomas Chan won heat one of the men's 100m backstroke, while Cook Islands' Carter Makira was third in heat two, ahead of Fiji's Don Younger in fourth.

Heat three saw Fiji's Samuela Yalimaiwai in fifth position while Samoa's Christian Toia was eighth.

In the men's 50m freestyle heats, Tonga's Finau Ohuafi finished first in heat 3 ahead of Vanuatu's Leo Lebot in second, while Fiji's Reuben Taylor won heat 4, which also had PNG's Josh Tarere in fourth and his countryman Thomas Chen in seventh.

Fijian pair David Young and Hansel McCaig both competed in heat 8, with Young finishing second while McCaig was eighth.

The women's 100m backstroke also saw a number of Pasifika swimmers, which included PNG's Joanna Chen claiming third in heat one, Samoa's Hamilton being second in heat two, with Cook Ilands' Mia Laban at fifth.

Netball

Tonga's Tala were thrashed 99-38 by Australia in their opening Pool A clash on Saturday night.

New Zealand defeated Scotland 74-44 in their opener.

The Games continue daily until 2 August.

As of 5pm on Sunday (NZT), Australia led the medal tally with 12 gold, five silver and five bronze.

World.title: Hospitals builds adopt new way to put digital infrastructure systems in place
World.content:
Two big hospital builds are adopting a new way of getting complex digital infrastructure systems put in place, with a tweak.

Whangārei and Nelson builds are adapting what the Dunedin redevelopment did when it hired a digital system integrator.

They are tweaking it slightly by putting the integrator under the main contractor instead directly with Health New Zealand.

Health NZ says getting hospital IT done this way recognises what a big job it is.

"It also aims to avoid perpetuating legacy technical issues by ensuring that contemporary, resilient digital infrastructure, aligned to Health New Zealand digital standards, is implemented on the major hospital build programmes," it said.

It was working successfully in Dunedin, it added.

Its tender alerting companies it will be hiring, invites them to join a list of pre-qualified suppliers for when the job is let for real.

It says that list may be used for other similar hospital projects in future.

World.title: Tottenham Hotspur beat Auckland FC 2-0 in pre-season friendly
World.content:
Tottenham Hotspur have beaten Auckland FC 2-0 in an entertaining pre-season friendly match at Eden Park in Auckland today.

Spurs, on a southern tour that includes two games in Australia, held a 1-0 lead at halftime, and doubled their tally in the second.

Spurs dictated early and their first goal to Dane Scarlett was due reward. It resulted from a terrific cross from Archie Gray to Manor Solomon who fired a shot which Auckland goalie Michael Woud stopped but couldn't hold and Scarlett pounced.

Auckland had their chances, and a Logan Rogerson pass found Sam Cosgrove late in the half, but goalie Brandon Austin was able to hold out his shot.

Both teams made numerous changes in the second half, with Spurs introducing some of their best talent..

One of them, Brazilian forward Richarlison, scored midway through the spell after a brilliant run from Mathys Tel set him up.

The match attracted a crowd of around 40,000 and was a boost for Spurs fans after they just survived Premier League relegation last season.

A-League victors Auckland were outclassed on a wet day, but will surely benefit from a game against Premier League opposition.

World.title: NZ Warriors scrape home with lucky win over Eels
World.content:
The Warriors have made it three wins from four matches with a frantic 14-12 victory over the Parramatta Eels in their NRLW clash Sydney today.

They had to do it in the hard way, after being down 12-4 in the 40th minute.

They fought back to a take a two point lead but then things went awry as they lost a player to the bin with four minutes to go and the Eels started to make big inroads against a struggling defence.

Dane Scarlett scores and celebrates his goal for Tottenham Hotspur against Auckland FC at Eden Park, Auckland, 26 July 2026. Photosport.nz

In the dying seconds the Eels looked to have stolen the game as Zali Fay went over in the left corner after an overlap but the officials ruled the final pass was forward and the home side's celebrations turned to despair.

The Warriors lacked the fluency of their play in their 42-4 win over the North Queensland Cowboys last weekend against opponents looking for their first win of the season.

But Patricia Maliepo's try in the 51st minute got them back on track, and Tysha Ikenasio handed the Eels a double blow just three minutes later.

The score stayed at 14-12 there, with the Warriors scraping in for a fortunate win.

World.title: Christchurch Catholic Diocese unveils plans for new $80m Cathedral of the Blessed Sacrament
World.content:
The design of Christchurch's new $80 million Catholic cathedral has been unveiled.

The Cathedral of the Blessed Sacrament is being built on the Barbadoes Street site of the 1905 original, which was demolished in 2020 after suffering irreparable damage in the 2010 and 2011 earthquakes.

The damaged Christchurch Catholic Basilica, 2019. Peter Fleming

The Catholic Diocese of Christchurch wants to raise $16m from parishioners to help fund the project.

In a pastoral letter on Sunday, Bishop Michael Gielen appealed to Catholic families in Canterbury and on the West Coast to financially contribute.

Gielen announced in 2024 the cathedral would return to the diocese's traditional home on Barbadoes Street and that it would retain the name Cathedral of the Blessed Sacrament.

A design rendering for Christchurch's new Cathedral of the Blessed Sacrament. Supplied / Catholic Diocese of Christchurch

He said that in the two years since significant work had been undertaken to develop the design in partnership with the architecture firm Warren and Mahoney.

"When I arrived in the diocese four years ago, one of the questions I was most often asked was: 'What is happening with the cathedral?'. That question revealed something profound, the deep love our people have for their Mother Church," Gielen said.

"Over these past four years, through listening, prayer and discernment, that shared vision has taken shape."

"It is an ancient design, a Romanesque and Gothic hybrid model. So that's drawing on the best of humanity's learnings over the centuries, that's beautiful to connect to that."

A design rendering for Christchurch's new Cathedral of the Blessed Sacrament. Supplied / Catholic Diocese of Christchurch

Gielen believed people would see in the design: "a cathedral that glorifies God, that serves as a beacon of faith in our city, that responds to the realities of the present day".

The diocese's cathedral campaign manager, Tony Brazier, said the project had an $80m budget that would cover the 800-seat cathedral, the attached perpetual adoration chapel and the Te Rangimarie community centre.

Brazier said about $45m of the funds needed to build the cathedral would come from insurance proceeds and the sale of diocesan assets.

Of the $35m required through fundraising, more than $19m had already been found, he said.

The proposed site of the Cathedral of the Blessed Sacrament. RNZ / Nate McKinnon

"Bishop Michael is emulating what Bishop Grimes did, inviting every Catholic family to make a sacrificial offering to build our new cathedral," he said

Gielen said he had heard from many people who had a sense of pride that their grandparents or great-grandparents helped fund the construction of the original Cathedral of the Blessed Sacrament.

"It's now our turn to answer the ancient call to build something that will last for generations," he said.

The Cathedral of the Blessed Sacrament, Christchurch, as it looked in 2005. Wikimedia Commons

"I have been struck by the generosity of people who recognise what a sign of hope our cathedral will be for Christchurch and our region. That generosity has been seen around New Zealand and from people of other faith traditions."

The diocese said that when half of the remaining $16m had been raised, the project would move towards final preparations for construction.

"We're only $8m short of pressing go on the build, so I'm very hopeful that people will get in behind it," Gielen said.

The cathedral will be the first new Catholic cathedral in New Zealand in 120 years.

Lead architect for the cathedral, Joseph Hampton, said he was honoured to be involved with the project.

"My great-great-great-grandfather donated to the first cathedral built, and my family has been involved in the parish throughout the years," he said.

"We received a really rich brief from the bishop and his amazing advisory group, so from there we started with master planning and making sure we arranged the site in a way that allows the campus to feel alive for the next 20, 50, 150 years.

"It's a cathedral that's grounded in tradition but built for Christchurch today."

World.title: Fozball and finals on the brink as Cronulla maul Manly
World.content:
Manly's hopes of a fairytale NRL finals berth are on life support after an insipid 48-12 loss to Cronulla, who appear genuine premiership contenders.

The Sea Eagles suffered their worst defeat of the Kieran Foran era as Sharks halves Nicho Hynes and Braydon Trindall lit up Brookvale Oval.

The 10th-placed Sea Eagles (9-10) have a losing record for the first time since round six and must win at least four of their last five regular-season games to play finals.

They are four competition points out of the top eight and face top-eight sides Newcastle, the Dolphins and Warriors on the run home.

It's been quite the fall from grace for the Sea Eagles, who rose from the doldrums and won eight of 10 games immediately after Foran replaced Anthony Seibold.

Manly have since lost five of six, and for the first time since club legend Foran became coach in March, they were never in the contest on Sunday.

The Sea Eagles' playmakers gave away four seven-tackle sets with poor kicks.

Reuben Garrick sprayed the kick-off out on the full after the Sharks' fourth try and put the visitors in place for Sione Katoa to score their fifth only minutes before the half.

Tom Trbojevic's replacement Lehi Hopoate had an afternoon to forget at fullback, notably spilling a regulation Hynes kick directly ahead of the Sharks' third try.

The fourth-placed Sharks have won eight from their last nine games and look ready to take the leap from good to great in Craig Fitzgibbon's fifth season as coach.

So long a lightning rod for criticism, halfback Hynes is playing as well as he has since winning the Dally M Medal in 2022.

He embarrassed the Manly middle barging over for the Sharks' fourth try and sent a bullet-like pass for Ronaldo Mulitalo's second try just after the break.

Hynes dummied through rookie five-eighth Joey Walsh, who had a difficult day, and then passed inside for Sifa Talakai to score in the second half.

He also kicked a career-best 26th consecutive goal and finished the afternoon with three line breaks.

Trindall's suspect ball to Teig Wilton gave Cronulla their opening try, before the five-eighth floated a lovely cut-out pass for Mulitalo's first.

He kicked past Hopoate for KL Iro to cross with 15 minutes to play.

Just before halftime, the Sea Eagles lost second-rower Ben Trbojevic to his second game-ending head knock in as many appearances.

Earlier, the makings were all there for another devastating Gold Coast loss, but coach Josh Hannay has credited the Titans' ongoing evolution for their slashing 38-18 win over St George Illawarra.

With the Dragons celebrating co-captain Clint Gutherson's 250th NRL game on Sunday afternoon, the permanent signing of coach Dean Young and Old Boys' Day to boot, the visitors had to overcome an early deficit to secure consecutive wins for the first time in the Hannay era.

Gold Coast's 20-point win allowed them to leapfrog three other clubs, and out of the competition's bottom four for the first time since their round-eight bye, and all but confirmed the Dragons' maiden wooden spoon.

"When you're coming into an environment like this, it felt like we were walking into a trap with them having so much to play for, so I just loved how we went about it," Hannay said.

"We have had some tight losses and haven't had a lot of reward at different times. There have been a few instances where we have had a level game at halftime and we'd flinch in the second half. I feel like this group, little by little, are growing.

"We're fully aware of where we're at, the journey we're on and that there's going to be some hard lessons. They have had to learn a lot on the run these guys and they're growing exponentially."

World.title: Lion's 'stupid action' sparks war of words as Nasiah magic inspires Saints
World.content:
Brisbane defender Ty Gallop faces an anxious wait on the match review officer after a contentious incident in the second quarter of the Lions' heavy win over Port Adelaide at the Gabba.

The emerging Gallop had rolled Mitch Georgiades in a heavy tackle, but while the Power key forward's head did not hit the turf, it was what happened next that raised eyebrows.

As the Lions swept the ball downfield, Gallop appeared to lift Georgiades by the jumper before slamming him back into the turf head first.

While Georgiades played out the game uninjured, he was returning from an earlier concussion against St Kilda in round 18 after being knocked out in a heavy mid-air collision.

The incident spurred a defensive reaction from both coaches after the match, with Port's Josh Carr saying Gallop's actions were the mark of a team that played its football on the edge.

"It wasn't a great look, but I'm on the other side of it," he said.

"They're a team that plays tough and pushes the limits. We got the free kick, so we got rewarded. There's not much more to say."

Carr said Georgiades was unaffected by the incident after the game.

But the coach's words spurred a response from his counterpart Chris Fagan, who said he hadn't seen the incident.

Asked if he agreed with Carr's assessment that his team played on the edge, Fagan said: "That's his opinion. He's allowed to have it.

"You don't be one of the better teams of the competition if you don't play a hard physical brand.

"That's what we do. I don't think we do it unfairly. I think we brought good pressure today."

Brisbane Lions great Alastair Lynch was also unimpressed by Gallop's actions, citing Georgiades's history with concussions as well.

"That's just a stupid action. We don't want to see that," he said on Fox Footy's coverage.

"Mitch [Georgiades] has had some problems with concussion and we don't want to see actions like that."

Fagan said he had yet to view a replay of the incident.

"It's interesting that Josh has had a chance to watch it; I haven't. He's not as busy as what I am," he said.

Fagan said he was hopeful defender Darcy Gardiner was available next week should Gallop be suspended.

"It's not really up to me; it's up to what the match review mob [and] what they decide," he said.

In Sunday's second match, St Kilda ran out 13.15 (93) to 8.14 (62) winners over North Melbourne as Nasiah Wanganeen-Milera finished with 46 disposals and four goals.

AAP

World.title: Tim Tszyu beats Errol Spence Jr by unanimous decision
World.content:
Tim Tszyu has beaten Errol Spence Jr in a blockbuster non-title middleweight boxing match in Sydney by unanimous decision, with the American great retiring in the ring post-fight.

All three judges scored the bout in favour of the Australian, 118-110, 117-111, 117-111, who moves to a 28-3 professional record, while handing Spence his second consecutive defeat.

"I had sleepless nights … how am I gunna feel facing a legend like that," Tszyu said in the ring.

"I understand why he is one of the greats.

"I wanna win a world title, but beating a great like Errol Spence tops any world title for me."

Tim Tszyu controlled the middle portion of the fight against Errol Spence Jr. (Getty Images: Brendon Thorne)

Tszyu controlled proceedings from the middle portion of the contest, marching down the former champion, who looked as rusty as you might expect from a man who has spent three years out of the ring.

Spence, a former unified world welterweight world champion, had not fought since 2023 when he suffered the first defeat of his professional career against Terrence Crawford, who was ringside in Sydney.

In his time out the ring, Spence was in a car crash that could have claimed his career, if not more.

But Tszyu, the larger man despite fighting at middleweight for the first time, was able to use his size to dictate the fight, marching down Spence and cutting off the ring.

Spence gave Tszyu's body a thorough examination in the opening rounds off the back of a clever jab and canny left hook, but the 36-year-old ran out of steam as the fight went on.

There were signs throughout that the former WBA, WBC and IBF champion was not the same fighter that he used to be, looking unsteady and unsure with his footwork.

As such, it was no real surprise that he revealed in the ring that he would not be continuing his fighting career.

"Congratulations to Tim, [coach] Jeff Fenech, it was a good showing by Tim" Spence said.

"I asked a lot of questions for myself. Now it's time to go home with my family and start a new life.

"I got my faculties intact, my money is good, it's working for itself, so everything's good.

"Now it's time to go home and life that family life."

It was all smiles between the two combatants after the fight. (Getty Images: Brendon Thorne)

Tszyu, who admitted to some dark thoughts about his career ahead of this fight, credited his new coach, Jeff Fenech, for forcing him to stick to his game plan.

"The two greats I'm trying to replicate are Kostya Tszyu and Jeff Fenech," Tszyu said.

"If I can get half as good as them, hey, I'll be sleeping as a great man.

Earlier, Commonwealth Games silver medallist and 2024 Paris Olympian Callum Peters earned a stoppage victory over Argentinian Luis Antonio Tejeda.

Tokyo Olympian Paulo Aokuso also secured victory via a spectacular 10th round knock out win despite struggling through the middle rounds against unbeaten Dominican Republic fighter Luis Antonio Tejeda.

In the co-main, veteran lightweight Paul Fleming was well beaten by unbeaten youngster Ahmad Reda via unanimous decision.

Paris Olympian Tina Rahimi beat Sacha Ryan Dryden for her first professional win as well.

Look back on how all the action unfolded in our live blog.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

World.title: No more tears left to cry as Godwin goes from hell to the mountaintop
World.content:
Four years ago, Georgia Godwin was at the peak of her powers as she led Australia to silver in the women's team final at the Birmingham Commonwealth Games.

She performed all four of the apparatus and had the highest score in three of them.

This time around, her first two rotations were just OK, aided by brilliant performances by Kate McDonald, whose 14.200 was the best uneven bars score of the day; and Breanna Scott on beam.

They backed it up on the floor, with first Scott, then McDonald posting the day's second-best scores on the apparatus.

Godwin was a picture of composure. (Getty Images: Naomi Baker)

Then Godwin reminded the world of her class with a stunning routine that earned her a 13.350 and left Australia in top spot with only the vault to come.

"There was a lot going through my head before that floor routine and the girls before me absolutely nailed their floors. I just really wanted to help the team and with all of that head noise and all of that pressure I just started feeling a bit overwhelmed," she said.

"So before I started floor, I went to my plans and grounded myself and I was so happy for that to be my first floor routine back at a big international event."

The moment her music faded out, the emotions came rushing into Godwin and out onto her face.

Georgia Godwin burst into tears immediately after her floor routine. (Getty Images: Owen Humphreys/PA Images)

Some mixture of pride and relief. Then the tears as she embraced every member of the team who had helped her get back.

The Achilles she tore two and a half years ago hadn't just held up, it had propelled her and her team towards almost certain gold in Glasgow.

Athletes often talk of resilience gained and lessons learned through adversity, but sometimes it just sucks to be unceremoniously kicked off the mountaintop, have your livelihood threatened and independence taken away.

"I'm gonna be completely honest, it's been a horrible, horrible road back," she said.

"My support team has been absolutely amazing, but the mental challenges I've had to go through have been the hardest I've been through in my life.

"But I want to finish this sport on my own terms and I wanted to do one more big event with these amazing girls.

The village got Georgia Godwin through hell. (Getty Images: Matthias Hangst)

"I've said it before and I'll say it over and over again, but it takes a village and I'm so lucky to have my special village."

That village includes her parents, who were in the stands to watch, her teammates, her coaches, physio, trainers, and of course puppy Remy.

Unsurprisingly, there were times when she thought she wouldn't be able to get back.

Too old, too sore, too hard. Just all too much.

It was too much again on Saturday night at the Glasgow International Arena.

The energy was high from the Australians throughout the final. (Getty Images: Naomi Baker)

Asked about her mindset as she stepped onto the floor, the emotions came for her again.

"I'm gonna have no tears left by the end of this," she laughed.

A solid 20 seconds of overwhelm later, she said she wasn't performing for herself but those dozens, hundreds of people who have helped her get back on the mat, the bars, the vault and the floor.

Five seconds later she was laughing about becoming Australia's most decorated female gymnast, and joking at the expense of Allana Slater.

It was another reminder of her ability to compartmentalise, albeit slightly less impressive than when she managed to compose herself after the ultimate release of sticking that floor routine to pull off a similarly superb 13.550 vault.

In a competition where they won gold by 1.1 point, a half misstep or misalignment could have seen the ultimate goal slip through her fingers again.

Georgia Godwin has returned to the top of the world. (Gety Images: Naomi Baker)

"My emotions don't come up very often but when they do I'm very good at suppressing them if I've got a job to do," she said.

"I think it's so important to feel your emotions but there's also a time and place, so I took the moment, got myself into a quiet corner and just laid down and tried to calm myself back down and did the job."

Job done, but not really.

Still ahead of her in Glasgow are gold medal defences in the all-around and vault finals, and a floor final.

But today isn't about any of that.

Today is about reminding her who she is, what she can do, and why she does it.

"I think everything is all good," she said.

"We can move on and I've really taken a step today."
